### 2026-10-26 — Crop corners resize in every direction — COMPLETE (0.0.662)

- **What was reported.** Dragging a corner did not resize the frame on the Firm Logo page.
- **Why.** Two faults in the corner math. The left corners read a downward drag as growth (the vertical direction was inverted), and the new width was taken from whichever axis was further from the pinned corner — so on the wide 148:100 logo frame a sideways pull was held at its starting width by the untouched vertical side.
- **What changed.** The width now follows the drag's dominant direction measured from where the drag began: a sideways pull changes a wide frame's width directly and a vertical pull does the same through the shape's ratio. The left corners' vertical direction is corrected. The pinned opposite corner, the 512 px floor, the image-edge limit, moving the frame, rotate, Save and the 50 KB cap are unchanged.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; crop suite **9 passed** (new: a sideways logo pull and all four corners), Profile and Manage Firm suites pass, full `flutter test` **2,137 passed**.
- **No mockup** — the Select Image page has none.

### 2026-10-26 — The crop frame resizes by its corners — COMPLETE (0.0.661)

- **What was asked.** Let the user resize the selection frame by dragging a corner, like an ordinary cropper, while the stored picture stays under the same 50 KB cap. Set a sensible minimum so the 512 px target still gets enough source pixels, and change nothing else that already works.
- **What changed.** In `image_crop_screen.dart` the frame is no longer fixed. Each corner carries a 44 px drag area around a small white dot; a drag resizes the frame with the **opposite corner pinned**, the shape held (square for the profile, 148:100 for the logo) and the frame kept inside the displayed image. The floor is the width that still feeds the stored 512 px output — 512 source pixels times the display scale, capped by the image's own size — so a 1600 x 1200 picture can shrink to 512 px and a small picture cannot shrink at all. Rotating restarts from the largest frame for the new orientation. Moving the frame, rotating, Cancel/Save, the saved-area mapping and the 50 KB/512 px pipeline are unchanged.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **2,135 passed**. New cases: a bottom-right drag on a 1600 x 1200 source stops at 512 source pixels, and a corner dragged far past the image edge leaves the saved area fully inside the image. The existing crop, processor, Profile and Manage Firm suites still pass.
- **No mockup** — the Select Image page is new and has none.

### 2026-10-26 — A chamber buyer keeps the seats before the firm exists — COMPLETE (0.0.645)

- **What was reported.** A free user bought **Firm — 1 Month**; after approval Manage Plan still showed **Devices 1 of 1**. The account had `tier = firm` but `firm_id = null`, so it fell to the one-per-member device cap.
- **The ruling applied.** The owner pays for the seats, so a chamber-tier account with **no chamber** (an owner-designate) may use the tier's full slots for its own devices until an associate joins. Firm 5 / Firm Plus 10 / Enterprise 20.
- **Server.** `20261026130000_owner_designate_device_slots.sql` re-issues `device_cap`: a chamber owner still reads `slots − associates`, a seated associate 1, a capacity-signed-out associate 0, a chamber-tier account with no chamber its **full tier seat cap**, and non-chamber tiers their own caps. **Applied live** — the project now records **72 versions**; `supabase/tests/firm_capacity_test.sql` prints **CAPACITY OK** with the new owner-designate cases (including Pro 2 / Starter 1 / Free 1 unchanged).
- **Client.** The post-payment approval watch now **re-registers this device** when the subscription changes, so the device gate's cap (and Manage Plan's devices meter) picks up the new number without a relaunch. A cold start registers anyway. `device_cap_parity_test.dart` pins the new branch; the watch test asserts the gate refresh happens exactly once when the expiry changes.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **2,100 passed**; ledger regenerated to **72 migrations** and `--check` clean; the live account that reported the issue now reads `device_cap = 5`.
- **Docs.** Plan, Task 22, the manual checklist (new **Scenario 16** and §12.11 SQL check), `supabase/README.md`, and the capacity/device memories updated.
- **Remaining.** The physical check in Scenario 16 is outstanding. If the owner fills all five slots with their own devices, adding the first associate needs one device signed out first — the card's “5 devices **or** 4 associates”.

### 2026-10-26 — Renewals stop the post-payment watch too — COMPLETE (0.0.644)

- **What was asked.** Follow-up to 0.0.643: an **already-premium** renewal or plan change kept the 30-second polling until the ten-minute window even after the plan appeared, because the early stop only recognised free → premium.
- **What changed.** The watch now captures the account's **governing expiry** when it starts — the profile's for an individual, the firm's for a chamber account, through the same `resolveSubscriptionExpiry` the entitlement uses — and re-reads it after every **successful** refresh. Any change ends the watch on that beat, so renewals, upgrades and queued downgrades stop as quickly as a free → premium approval. The free → premium check remains only as the fallback when the start expiry could not be read; a failed refresh compares nothing. A rejection moves no expiry, so it still runs to the window. No server change.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **2,100 passed**; the new case starts with the account already premium and moves the expiry on the first beat — one refresh, then the watch is stopped and later beats do nothing (the old behaviour would have kept polling).
- **Remaining.** A rejected payment still polls to the ten-minute limit; stopping on the ledger's resolution (one extra read per tick) was considered and not added.

### 2026-10-26 — An approval applies itself without a sign-out — COMPLETE (0.0.643)

- **What was reported.** After a free user bought a plan and an admin approved it, the app kept showing **Free** for minutes; only signing out and back in applied the plan.
- **Why.** A free account deliberately holds no Realtime socket (sync is entitlement-gated) and there is no approval push, so nothing told the app. Its profile cache is re-read only on launch, resume, reconnect or sign-in — none of which happens while the payer waits in the app.
- **What changed.** The checkout now starts a bounded watch after a confirmed submission (`payment_approval_watch.dart`): every **30 seconds for 10 minutes** it re-reads the account — pulling the profile and firm and recomputing premium — and invalidates both Subscription History ledgers on the same beat, so the plan, gates and pending row update while the payer waits. It stops early when a free account turns premium, pauses while the app is backgrounded (the resume refresh covers that), and a second submission restarts the window. No server change; no new copy.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **2,099 passed**; new tests cover the 30-second beat, the end of the window, a restart, and the checkout starting the watch.
- **Remaining.** An approval that lands after the 10-minute window, or after the app was killed and relaunched before the approval, still relies on the existing launch/resume refresh. Covering those automatically would need a server-side approval signal (a broadcast for socket-holding accounts or an approval push), which is a separate piece of work.

### 2026-10-25 — The storage policies are live and both proofs pass — COMPLETE (0.0.634)

- **What was done.** The owner created the eight policies in the Supabase Storage policy editor. The editor automatically added a SELECT policy beside each UPDATE and DELETE policy — the Storage API reads a row before it writes or removes it. All twelve are **permissive**, role `authenticated`; the extra SELECTs are redundant with each bucket's base SELECT and add no restriction. UPDATE policies use their `USING` expression as `WITH CHECK` because no separate check was given, which is the correct PostgreSQL behaviour.
- **Verified live:** twelve policies (8 base + 4 auto SELECT), all permissive and authenticated; names carry a cosmetic dashboard suffix (`… bf2ca3_0` / `… xbqzuu_0`).
- **Proofs fixed and green.** Two test assumptions were wrong and are corrected: PostgreSQL strings escape a quote with `''`, not `\'`; and a lapsed owner's UPDATE is **filtered to 0 rows** by `USING` rather than raising an error. The proofs also set `storage.allow_delete_query = true` for their transaction, the same flag the Storage API uses for its own deletes. Both ran against the project: **FIRM LOGO OK**, **PROFILE AVATAR OK**.
- **Live state:** 69 migrations; both buckets at 50 KB/JPEG; all four columns, helper functions and triggers; both Edge Functions active; the policy set above.
- **Checks.** `flutter analyze` clean; full suite **2,064 passed**; ledger regenerated (manual note added) and its tests green. Version **0.0.634**.
- **Remaining:** a device smoke test — premium individual uploads, a second device downloads, delete propagates; owner sets a chamber logo and an associate sees it; lapsed/free/member restrictions; account deletion on a throwaway account removes `{user_id}.jpg`.

### 2026-10-23 — The Email domain window stays put and reads as the address — COMPLETE (0.0.609)

- **What was asked.** Four corrections to the Login and Sign Up Email box's domain window: a touch that holds and scrolls must not close it (only a plain tap should); it must stay visible while the user holds and scrolls; it must always hang under the Email box rather than flipping above it, scrolling the box up when the keyboard leaves no room; and every row must show the text the user typed before the domain.
- **What changed** (only `auth_widgets.dart` and its test file, no other screen).
  - **Dismissal is decided on lift.** The window's `TapRegion` records the outside press and waits for the lift; it closes only when the finger did not travel past `kTouchSlop`. A scroll of the page, or a hold that scrolls, leaves the window up, and the follower keeps it attached to the box as the page moves.
  - **Always below the box.** The "above when the keyboard leaves no room" branch is gone. On show (and on a keystroke that changes the list), a post-frame check measures the shortfall between the room under the box and the list's height and scrolls the enclosing page up by it, clamped to the page's own scroll range; a page that cannot give enough still gets an internally scrolling window.
  - **The floor is read from the view.** The Scaffold body's `MediaQuery` has the keyboard inset removed, while the overlay window's does not; the scroll check now reads `MediaQueryData.fromView` so both agree (the first build measured 640 px against the window's 340 and never scrolled).
  - **Rows are whole addresses.** Each row renders `localPart + domain` (`john@gmail.com`), keyed as before by the domain, and a pick still replaces anything typed after the `@`.
- **Tests.** `auth_email_field_test.dart` now has 13: the existing 10 plus the typed-name rows, holding and scrolling keeps the window while a tap closes it, and a small viewport with a fake keyboard inset proves the page scrolls the box up, the window stays under it and its foot stays above the keyboard floor. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1986 passed**; version **0.0.609** recorded.

### 2026-10-23 — The Daily Cause List's month/year spin is heard — COMPLETE (0.0.607)

- **What was asked.** Scrolling the Month | Year columns in the Daily Cause List's calendar played no sound. It should play the same sound the Notification Time window plays, and only when a month or year actually moves. Scope was the Daily Cause List only, so no other picker may change.
- **Why it was silent.** Those columns played Flutter's `SystemSoundType.click`, which the phone's own touch-sound setting decides whether to play at all; with that setting off the spin made no sound. The Notification Time window instead plays a bundled `sounds/gear_click.wav` through `audioplayers` in low-latency mode, which no phone setting can suppress.
- **What changed.**
  - `calendar_picker_dialog.dart` (the Daily Cause List's calendar) now plays that same bundled tick, through the same asset and the same low-latency mode, once for each month or year the columns move to: the tick fires from the columns' own `onChanged`, which only reports a row that has moved into the middle. Opening or closing the columns, a tap on the row the wheel already holds, the header's ‹ › arrows and the day-grid swipe stay silent — the month the columns open on is remembered as already heard, so confirming it does not tick again.
  - `month_year_picker.dart` gained `playRowClick` (default true, plumbed through both columns), so this calendar can switch the platform click off and play one tick rather than a click plus a tick. Every other picker keeps the click unchanged.
- **Tests.** 1 new in `test/shared/widgets/phase4_widgets_test.dart`: opening the selector is silent, one year move ticks once, one month move ticks once, confirming the row the wheel holds does not tick again, and no `SystemSound.play` joins it while moving (a mocked platform channel proves it — a tap's own feedback click is cleared before the spin so it cannot be mistaken for a row click). The whole dialog group now counts ticks instead of playing them, because the audio plugin must never be touched in a widget test. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1973 passed**; version **0.0.607** recorded.

### 2026-10-23 — Pull-to-sync on every routed screen, and the page no longer moves — COMPLETE (0.0.606)

- **What was asked.** The user wanted a premium account to be able to pull down to sync on every screen and sub-menu, running exactly the header Sync action, without going back to a case list. The agreed scope was **routed screens only**: dialogs, bottom sheets, the note editor with an unsaved draft, auth, paywall and checkout are excluded.
- **What changed.**
  - New shared `lib/shared/widgets/pull_to_sync.dart`: a premium-gated `RefreshIndicator` that runs `SyncService.retryNow()` and then the page's own reload when it has one. It is inert for free and unknown entitlement; a widget test without a `ProviderScope` still renders (the gesture is simply absent).
  - `SettingsSubPageModal` wraps every sub-page body in it, so all ~40 Settings pages, Account & Profile, Profile, Online Sync, Sync Status, courts, language, legal documents and subscription screens sync from their own body. Admin Payment Requests, Unconfirmed Accounts and Backup & Restore opt out (`pullToSync: false`): the admin pages own a pull that syncs and reloads their server lists, and a sync must not start during a backup or restore.
  - Settings dashboard and Devices carry the same wrapper. Devices also re-reads the registry (`deviceGateProvider.refresh(claim: false)`).
  - All six case lists now call `pullCaseListToSync(ref, _loadCases)` (forced sync + reload, the header's action) and use `AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics`; Case Detail's pull does the same. Notes and Case Reference already synced and now take the shared clamped configuration, so a short library is pullable.
- **The bug the first build introduced.** The wrapper supplied `AlwaysScrollableScrollPhysics()` through a `ScrollConfiguration` with no parent. That physics has no bounds, so a short Settings page followed the finger and stayed wherever it was dropped; on Android 12+ the overscroll stretch also moved the whole page. `pullScrollBehavior(context)` now binds the always-scrollable physics to the platform physics and turns the overscroll effect off, so the content stays inside its bounds and only the refresh spinner moves. Pinned by `test/shared/widgets/pull_to_sync_test.dart`.
- **Tests.** A new `pull_to_sync_test.dart` (3): premium runs sync + reload, a short page stays at offset 0 with no stretch indicator, free gets no gesture. `daily_cause_list_test.dart` asserts the pull calls the sync engine. The Profile Details test now unmounts its tree before the test ends, because the premium gate's cached-profile watch is a Drift stream whose close timer otherwise stayed pending and stalled the rest of that file. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1972 passed**; version **0.0.606** recorded.

### 2026-10-23 — Revoked device rows are pruned after six months — COMPLETE (0.0.604)

- **The policy.** Keep every `user_devices` row from the last six months; never delete an active row; for each `(user_id, device_key)` keep the newest revoked row even when it is older than six months; delete only revoked rows older than six months that have a strictly newer revoked row for the same account/device key. Rows tied at the newest instant all survive. Age is `revoked_at`, never `last_seen_at` (the touch trigger rewrites that on every update).
- **Server — `20261023120000_user_devices_retention.sql`, applied (67 versions).**
  - Partial index `user_devices_revoked_retention_idx (user_id, device_key, revoked_at desc) where revoked_at is not null` supports the newest-revoked lookup.
  - `public.prune_user_devices(p_retention interval default interval '6 months')` is `security definer`, validates a positive interval, performs one set-based DELETE with a correlated “newer revoked row” check, reports the count and returns it.
  - It is **internal**: `revoke all ... from public, anon, authenticated`. The owner and pg_cron can execute. (`purge_tombstones` has a pre-existing grant gap; this deliberately does not copy it.)
  - pg_cron job **`prune-user-devices`** runs daily at **03:45**, after `purge-tombstones` at 03:15. The job is unscheduled-then-scheduled, so re-applying does not stack duplicates.
  - No delete runs in the migration; the first scheduled run performs it.
- **Proof.** `DEVICE OK` with 8 fixture deletions and 0 on a second run. It covers: old build-ID key with two phones, recent/old mix, tied newest rows, the exact six-month boundary, a NULL reason, `flushed_at`, a newer `last_seen_at`, old active rows, an active plus its only revoked row, two accounts sharing a key, separate install keys, and all-recent rows. It also asserts the grant deny for `anon`/`authenticated`, the definer/search_path, and both cron jobs.
- **Live.** 67 versions applied; both cron jobs active (`purge-tombstones` 03:15, `prune-user-devices` 03:45); `anon`/`authenticated` cannot execute the pruner; the pre-check for old non-newest rows is **0**.
- **Tests.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1967 passed**; ledger regenerated (67, `--check` clean); version **0.0.604** recorded.
- **Residual risks.** A token older than six months from a full clone kept alive could still look unknown after its row is pruned; the newest revoked row per key and the six-month window make that unlikely. One permanent row remains per historical install key (reinstalls add keys). The **18 recent test rows survive** — the policy only removes rows older than six months; removing those test rows would be a separate owner-approved cleanup.

### 2026-10-23 — The third device's first Sign Out no longer hits Could Not Check — COMPLETE (0.0.603)

- **The report.** On a third phone at the **Device Limit Reached** window, the first **Sign Out** tap produced *Could Not Check This Device*; **Try Again** showed the window again, and the second Sign Out worked.
- **What the live data proved.** The sign-outs themselves succeeded: each target row is `revoked_reason = signed_out`, and the third device's own row was created in the same second. The Postgres log shows no `sign_out_device`/`register_device` error at that time. So the failure was not the server and not the stale build-ID collision from 0.0.600.
- **The actual cause — a client race introduced with the push.** A phone on the full-plan window holds **no `user_devices` row**. The new forced check (a channel join, or another device's revocation broadcast) could run on it: `touch_device` answered `not_active`, `device_state` answered `unregistered`, and the gate renders `unregistered` as *Could Not Check This Device*. The sign-out's own re-registration had already freed the slot and admitted the phone, but the stray check overwrote the screen until Try Again registered again.
- **The fix.** `DeviceGateController.touch` now runs only when the gate is **active** (after the signed-in guard). A phone that holds no slot is not revoked — it is refused — so the window's **Sign Out → register** is the authority for it. A genuinely revoked device is still `active` until the check discovers it, so it still receives the push and discards.
- **Tests.** New controller test: a gate in `limitReached` ignores a forced check and makes no repository call. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1965 passed**; version **0.0.603** recorded. No server change and no migration.
- **What the user should see now.** On the third phone, the **first** Sign Out should admit it (the slot is freed by the sign-out's register); the removed phone still signs out immediately from its own broadcast.

### 2026-10-23 — A revoked phone is told by Realtime, not by polling — COMPLETE (0.0.602)

- **What changed.** The 30-second foreground timer is **removed**. When a `user_devices` row turns revoked, a database trigger sends the app's existing `row_change` `{table,id}` ping on the private topic the device actually joined; the listener routes a `user_devices` ping to one light `touch_device` check per 400 ms burst, never to the sync pull. Launch registration, a **forced** resume check, a **forced** check on every channel join/rejoin, and the existing refused-push re-read remain.
- **Server — `20261023110000_device_revocation_broadcast.sql`, applied (66 versions).**
  - `public.broadcast_device_revoked()` sends only on the null → non-null `revoked_at` transition, so heartbeats, re-registration, wipe acknowledgements and the identity backfill stay silent.
  - Topic: `firm:<firm_id>` when the owner's profile holds a firm (the app's firm-mode channel), otherwise `user:<user_id>`. A `user:`-only send would have missed every chamber member.
  - The send is wrapped in its own exception block: a Realtime failure logs a warning and **never rolls back the revocation**.
  - The proof prints **DEVICE OK** with new checks: the individual topic, no second message for an already-revoked row, and the firm topic (and not the user topic) for a firm member.
- **Client.**
  - `RealtimeListener` gains optional `onDeviceChanged` and `onSubscribed` callbacks; a `user_devices` ping is coalesced with the existing 400 ms window and never reaches `onPings`. `onSubscribed` fires once per successful join, including a rejoin — the recovery boundary for a broadcast missed while the socket was down.
  - `sync_providers.dart` schedules the gate check in a microtask, reads the notifier lazily and guards `ref.mounted`, so a socket callback can never re-enter a provider that is signing out.
  - `DeviceGateController.touch({bool force})`: ordinary checks keep the 30-second de-duplication window; resume, rejoin and a device ping force past it. The label retry and the `not_active → refresh` branch stay.
  - `SyncTriggerScope` no longer owns a timer; its resume check is forced.
- **Tests.** New listener tests (routing, burst coalescing, pending drop, join/rejoin callback), a controller test (de-duplication, forced bypass, `not_active` revocation, thrown-check reset, signed-out no-op), a provider-wiring test (deferred, forced, dropped after dispose) and a resume widget test. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1964 passed**; version **0.0.602** recorded.
- **Battery/cost.** No 30-second requests remain. A revocation adds one broadcast per active device and one light check per device on the rare event; the per-device channel was already open in the foreground.
- **Manual verification still required.** Phone B open and healthy, sign out from A's Devices window → B discards immediately (about a second). Background B, revoke again → no change until B is foregrounded, then the forced resume check discards. Airplane mode on B, revoke from A, restore connectivity → the rejoin check discards. Confirm PostgREST logs show no 30-second pattern while the app idles in front.

### 2026-10-23 — The label heals itself, and a revoked phone signs out while open — COMPLETE (0.0.601)

- **Why the first Redmi Note 10 Pro still read *Unknown device*.** The live row confirmed it: the active row for that phone (`c3e69961…`) has the stored UUID key (the 0.0.600 key fix worked), but `platform = unknown` and `label = Unknown device`. That launch's model lookup timed out (the 2-second cap) and the registration wrote the fallback. The label is only written when a device **registers**, and that phone was resumed rather than relaunched, so nothing rewrote it. The second phone's lookup answered and stored `Xiaomi M2101K6G`. No server change is needed: the label just needs another registration with the model.
- **The fix.** On the foreground heartbeat, if the cached identity is the generic fallback, the app re-asks the platform (bypassing the cached answer) and, when it gets the model, invalidates the identity and **re-registers**, which updates the row's label. This retries every heartbeat until it succeeds, so the first phone's label becomes `Xiaomi M2101K6G` without a restart.
- **Why a signed-out phone stayed open.** The revocation was only noticed on app **resume**, after a push, or when the Devices screen opened. A phone already in the foreground on any other screen never re-checked, so the third device freeing a slot did not reach it. The 0.0.600 heartbeat already acted on `not_active`; it just was not called often enough.
- **The fix.** `SyncTriggerScope` now runs a **30-second foreground heartbeat**: it starts on launch and resume, stops on pause/hidden/detached, and is cancelled with the scope. Each tick calls `touch_device`; when the server answers `not_active`, the gate re-reads `device_state`, shows the revocation and starts the discard. A signed-out phone therefore leaves the diary within 30 seconds while it is open, and on its next resume if it was backgrounded. The Devices screen's own read remains.
- **Tests.** A new test advances the clock 31 seconds and asserts the heartbeat asks the gate; the label path is covered by the identity tests. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1954 passed**; version **0.0.601** recorded.
- **What the user must do.** Install **0.0.601** on the phones. The first Redmi Note 10 Pro's active row will correct itself to `Xiaomi M2101K6G` within 30 seconds of the app being in front (or on its next launch). The old revoked rows with *This device* / *Unknown device* are history.

### 2026-10-23 — Identical phones no longer collide, and each device row says who owns it — COMPLETE (0.0.600)

- **The report, and what the live data showed.** On the Pro account, the second Redmi Note 10 Pro was refused, sign-out from the window said *Could not sign out this device*, the RN11 only signed out when the Devices screen was opened, and the final login left the app on *Could Not Check This Device* with no sync. The live `user_devices` rows and Postgres log gave the cause: `device_info_plus`'s Android `id` is the **build ID**, not the SSAID, and both Redmi Note 10 Pro handsets report `SKQ1.210908.001`. The second phone therefore failed the one-active-row-per-key index (`user_devices_active_device_idx`, SQLSTATE 23505) on every registration. That 500 is what made the check, the sign-out refresh and sync fail. Several rows also carried `label = "This device"` and a random UUID because the two-second identity timeout used a per-process key. The `touch_device` answer (`not_active`) was ignored, which is why the revoked RN11 stayed on its diary until the Devices screen asked the server.
- **Client — a key that is actually this install's.** `DeviceIdentityService` now reads a **persisted UUID from SharedPreferences** before the plugin and uses it as the key on Android and Windows; iOS keeps `identifierForVendor` when it answers and falls back to the same UUID. The Android build ID is no longer used. The timeout no longer mints a per-process key: it reuses the stored key and the **last model name** the plugin reported, so a slow launch cannot create a new device. A model label is remembered on every successful resolve; the generic label is now **Unknown device**, never *This device*. The phone's own row still reads **Xiaomi M2101K6G · This device** because the Devices screen appends the localized suffix for the current device; Supabase stores only the model.
- **Client — honest sign-out and a heartbeat that acts.** `revoke_device`/`sign_out_device` answering `already_revoked` now counts as success, so a second tap no longer shows *Could not sign out*. `touch_device` now returns whether the device is still active; when the server says no, the gate re-reads `device_state` and starts the discard immediately, so a revoked phone signs out on its next resume instead of waiting for the Devices screen. `touch`/`refresh` skip when signed out, which also stops the `permission denied` noise from calls made as `anon`.
- **Server — `20261023100000_device_identity_and_collision_guard.sql`, applied (65 versions).**
  - `user_devices` gains **`full_name`** and **`email`**, filled from `profiles` by a `BEFORE INSERT` trigger and backfilled for every existing row. Live check: 9 of 9 rows carry both.
  - `register_device` answers a key already held by another active device with **`device_limit_reached`** instead of inserting into a unique violation; the existing phone keeps working and the new sign-in can free the slot from the window.
  - A known session re-registering with a key another active row holds **keeps its own key** and still returns `ok`, instead of failing the index.
- **Proof.** `supabase/tests/device_limit_test.sql` prints **DEVICE OK** with two new sections: a row carries the account holder's name and e-mail, and a colliding key is refused as a full plan (one active row, the first device untouched) while a known session cannot steal another row's key. Ledger regenerated (65 migrations, `--check` clean), count guards and `versions.last` updated, the old registry migration gained a correction pointer. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1953 passed** (two new identity tests); version **0.0.600** recorded.
- **What the user must do.** Install **0.0.600** on both Redmi Note 10 Pro phones. The phone already signed in updates its row's key on launch; the second phone logs in and gets its own key, so both appear in Devices and sync. The old revoked rows labelled *This device* are history and need no action. If a phone still shows *Could Not Check*, its build is older than 0.0.600.
- **Still not verified on hardware.** The identity key is proven by unit tests and the server guard by SQL; the two-phone pass remains for the user.

### 2026-10-22 — A sign-in now belongs to one phone, and the heartbeat is wired — COMPLETE (0.0.595)

- **What changed.** Each install creates a random secret once, keeps it only on that phone, and sends it with every server call. The server stores a scrambled copy (SHA-256), not the secret. If the same sign-in is presented from a different phone, the server answers **session_in_use** instead of accepting it, and that phone discards its local copy and shows Login. A registration with **no** secret is refused outright (`invalid_install_secret`) and lands on the same discard screen, so a caller cannot skip the binding.
- **Same phone, new sign-in.** `replaced` — the one case that keeps local data — now requires both the same device key **and** the same install secret. A restored backup carries the key but not the this-device-only secret, so it is correctly treated as a **new device**, not the old one.
- **Heartbeat.** The app now calls `touch_device` when it returns to the foreground and after a successful sync, at most once an hour, so the seven-day idle eviction measures real use rather than app launches.
- **Secure storage.** The Supabase session and the install secret use this-device-only storage (`FlutterSecureKeyStorage.sessionOnly()`): iOS `first_unlock_this_device`, Android's default Keystore-backed ciphers. The database key deliberately keeps the default constructor.
- **Server.** `20261022160000_device_install_secret.sql`: adds `user_devices.install_secret_hash`, `current_install_secret()`/`current_install_hash()`, re-issues `register_device` (4 args; the old 3-arg form is dropped), `device_state`, `device_may_push`, `device_may_read` and `touch_device`. Push and heartbeat fail closed on a mismatch; reads keep a **permissive fallback when no secret is present** because Realtime does not reliably forward custom headers — an accepted residual risk, documented in the migration.
- **Applied live** to `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` — **64 of 64 versions recorded**. The refreshed body was re-applied directly with `psql` after the proof caught a gap (a registration that omitted the parameter never bound the row); the fix falls back to the header and refuses a secret-less registration.
- **Proof.** `supabase/tests/device_limit_test.sql` prints **DEVICE OK** with new checks: only the hash is stored, a different secret answers `session_in_use`, `device_state` reports it, a clone cannot push or read, a missing secret is refused, the real install still registers, and a restored copy does not become `replaced`. Ledger regenerated (64 migrations), `--check` clean, both count guards and `versions.last` updated.
- **Tests.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1948 passed**; version **0.0.595** recorded with the script. Plan and Task 22 updated per rule 14.
- **Known limits (plain).** A stolen sign-in that connects **before** the real phone reconnects after this update can still claim that row once — the row has no secret yet to compare against. A full copy of both the sign-in and the secret cannot be told apart from the original phone. Reads from Realtime may not carry the secret, so they stay open while writes stay closed.
- **Device pass still outstanding.** Two Pro phones plus a third sign-in: refused window, sign-out one device, discard on the removed phone, same-phone re-login keeps data, restored copy is refused, and the idle eviction still fires after seven days.

### 2026-10-22 — Audited the silent gear tick — COMPLETE (0.0.587)

- **The question.** Why is there still no sound while the time picker's hand is dragged?
- **What the audit proved.** A fresh **debug APK** contains `assets/sounds/gear_click.wav` (and its `AssetManifest` entry) and registers the `audioplayers` plugin. The drag listener is reached in widget tests, and the tick's WAV is valid (44.1 kHz mono, 55 ms, peak 0.82). So the code path and packaging are correct in a full build.
- **The most likely reason: a stale install.** Adding a native plugin and a new asset needs a full stop and rebuild. Hot reload/restart cannot register `audioplayers` or bundle the sound, and the old catch swallowed the resulting error, so the failure looked exactly like silence.
- **Other possibilities.** The phone's **media stream volume is zero**, or audio goes to a muted Bluetooth route. The tick is on the media stream; iOS silent mode is bypassed by default.
- **One real weakness found.** The audio call caught every error silently, and the first tick loads the asset while the code stops/replays on each 80 ms step; on a slow first load a very short drag can be silent.
- **Diagnostics added.** A debug build now prints **Gear tick: hand drag detected** on the first tick of a drag, and **Gear tick failed: …** with the stack if the audio call throws. If neither line appears, the running app is not this build.
- **Next step.** Run a full `flutter run` (stop the old app first), drag the hand with media volume up, and report the console line if it is still silent.
- **Proof.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1941 passed**; version **0.0.587** recorded with the script.

### 2026-10-21 — An install that has not updated can back up again — COMPLETE (0.0.567)

- **What was wrong.** The device limit's roll-out promise was half kept. Reads let an unregistered session through until 2026-11-21; writes did not, so an install from before the limit could pull the account's diary down and could not hand a single edit back up. Its first push was refused as `device_revoked`, and because a refusal is not retryable the client marked every queued change `blocked` — visible in Sync Status as *The server refused this change*, and never sent again on its own. Nothing was deleted, but a lawyer's backup had quietly stopped.
- **The fix.** `supabase/migrations/20261022130000_device_push_rollout_window.sql` gives `device_may_push` the same branch as `device_may_read`, on the same date: a session with **no `user_devices` row at all** may push until `device_rollout_end()`. Revocation in this registry stamps `revoked_at` on a row and never deletes it, so the branch cannot admit a device the server revoked — that device keeps exactly its 14-day flush window. After the date both gates close together.
- **Proof.** Four checks added to `supabase/tests/device_limit_test.sql`: an unregistered session pushes inside the window, `push_changes` lets it through, a revoked device is still refused while that window is open, and after it an unregistered session is refused with `device_revoked`. `DEVICE OK` printed with psql exit 0 against `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau`; putting the pre-0.0.567 function back makes the proof fail on the first new check, so it depends on the branch rather than passing beside it. Migration applied — the project records **61 versions**. `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1934 passed**; ledger regenerated (61 migrations) and `--check` clean; both migration-count guards moved to 61 and `versions.last` to the new file.
- **Resume point, next session.** Still the two-phone pass in `docs/tasks/22_verification_plan.md` Phase 6: a third sign-in refused while both devices were used within a week, an idle spare (eight days) evicted and shown *This Device Was Signed Out*, a lapse erasing nothing, and a phone signing in on a known device reusing its slot.

### 2026-10-21 — The device limit is live, and its own proof caught a real bug — COMPLETE (0.0.566)

- **What the user asked for.** Apply the device-limit migrations to the live project `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` and run the SQL proof until it prints `DEVICE OK`.
- **Applied.** `dart run tool/apply_supabase_migrations.dart` applied `20261022100000_device_limit_registry` and `20261022110000_device_limit_enforcement` (57 → 59 recorded versions), so the limit is no longer inert: the tables, the RPCs, the read gates and the `push_changes` wrapper are on the live database.
- **The proof failed on its first run, and it was right to.** A third sign-in on a two-device Pro account came back *ok*, and one of the two devices already holding a slot was revoked as `lapse`. Cause: `device_trim_surplus` kept `cap - 1` devices *other than the caller*, which is correct only when the caller already occupies a slot, and `register_device` trims before it knows whether it does. Effect in the field would have been that the plan-full screen could never appear and a working phone would be told the plan changed for no reason.
- **Fix.** `supabase/migrations/20261022120000_device_trim_counts_the_caller.sql` re-issues `device_trim_surplus` so it asks `user_devices` whether the caller holds an active row and subtracts its own slot only then. A new device leaves the whole cap to the devices present, so a full plan answers `device_limit_reached`; an account already above its cap is still trimmed back to it; nothing is revoked without a live plan, as before. Applied — the project now records **60 versions**.
- **Three defects were in the proof, not the server, and were repaired there.** It filled only one of a lapsed Pro's two slots and then expected a refusal (a lapse does not shrink the tier, so two rows are needed); it read `user_devices` as an authenticated session although the registry deliberately grants no read to any client role; and its roll-out-window pair set one window and then passed a date inside it, which cannot both hold — the window is now pushed to 2030 so the pair never goes stale.

### 2026-10-21 — The device limit is real: sign-ins are capped, spares are freed safely — COMPLETE (0.0.565)

- **What the user asked for.** The plans have always promised a number of devices in use at once — Pro two, every other plan one, and each chamber plan one per member — and nothing enforced it; `payment_plans.dart` even carried a comment saying so. The limit is now enforced on the server, and the app explains it.
- **The four rules the user set, in their own words.** A third device on a two-device plan **signs the least recently used device out automatically**; a device over the limit is **signed out and its local copy erased**; when a plan falls, **the phone in the lawyer's hand keeps working** and the spares go; and *one concurrent device each* on the chamber cards **includes the owner**.
- **The two consequences they ruled on next.** Unsent work is **saved before anything is erased**, and **nothing is erased on a lapse** (a lapsed account has nowhere to hand the work to and cannot restore an empty device). An automatic eviction needs the spare to have been **idle seven days or more**, because an offline phone can look idle while its owner is working on it.
- **How the cap is counted: sign-ins, not installs.** `user_devices` holds one row per session, keyed by the `session_id` claim in the access token — Supabase's own docs say every access token carries it, and a client cannot forge it — with the install's key beside it so the same phone signing in again reuses its slot. The install key alone would be client-supplied, and therefore worthless as a limit.
- **Server.** `20261022100000_device_limit_registry.sql` (the cap per tier, `device_cap` holding a chamber member to one, the registry, `register_device`'s decision table, `device_state`, `revoke_device`, `ack_device_wipe`, `device_trim_surplus` for a ceiling that fell, and `device_tokens.device_key`) and `20261022110000_device_limit_enforcement.sql` (`device_may_push` with a **14-day flush window** so a revoked device can still hand its work over, `device_may_read` added to the eleven ledger tables and `conflict_log`, and `push_changes` kept as `push_changes_core` behind a one-line device gate rather than re-typed).
- **App.** A `DeviceIdentityService` (Android SSAID, a stored install UUID elsewhere, with a two-second cap so a wedged platform channel cannot hold up registration), `DeviceGateScope` under the membership scope — a full plan names the devices holding the slots and frees one on request; a revoked device **flushes, acknowledges, then wipes and signs out**, and a failed flush erases nothing and says so — a **Devices** list under Manage Account, and `pushBeforeErase`/`_deviceMaySync` in the sync engine. A revoked device that is rejected mid-session re-reads its state instead of waiting for the next launch.
- **Copy follows the reason**, not one sentence for four situations: a fallen ceiling reads as a plan change, a removal as the lawyer's own action, a second sign-in as that sign-in ending, and a new device taking the slot as that. Bengali added for the three new sentences, and the Terms gained a **Devices** clause in both languages.
- **Roll-out.** Registrations past the cap are admitted and flagged `grandfathered` until **2026-11-21**, and `device_may_read` admits an unregistered session until the same date, so the update itself strands nobody and an install that has not updated keeps working. The client also treats a server with no registry at all (`PGRST202`) as "no limit here", so shipping the app before the SQL cannot stop syncing.
- **Proof.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1934 passed**, including the new `device_limit_test.dart` (Devices list, plan-full screen, revoked screen, and the reason-specific sentence) and `test/supabase/device_cap_parity_test.dart`, which pins the server's `tier_device_cap` to `SubscriptionTier.deviceCap` and the chamber rule. The ledger was regenerated (`59 migrations`) and its `--check` is clean. **The two migrations are written but not applied** — this host's `supabase/.env.local` still holds the password placeholder — and `supabase/tests/device_limit_test.sql` has therefore not been run against a database; until they are applied, the limit is inert and every install reads `unmanaged`.

### 2026-10-19 — The rpc smoke test is green again: it had stopped testing what it said — COMPLETE (0.0.548)

- **The request.** Close the last reported stale-SQL-test finding: `supabase/tests/rpc_smoke_test.sql` failed inside its removal fixture with `add_not_permitted`, even though the server behaviour it checks had not changed.
- **The cause — four drifts, all in the test, none in the server.** (1) The script returned to the server role with a bare `reset role`, which restores the role but leaves `request.jwt.claims` behind, so a fixture staged afterwards was judged as the previous member's write and refused. (2) The stale claims had also been *hiding* a real gap: the `not_found` approval check only answered as an admin because the claims from the block before it were still in force, so it was never stating the identity it needed. (3) The removal block staged its member as the real `user_id`, but `remove_firm_member` resolves the caller's chamber from `firms.owner_id` and that account already owns the chamber staged for `approve_payment` — so the call answered `not_found` and the associate's refusal was never exercised. (4) Two of its read-scope assertions still encoded the pre-`20261015100000_firm_mode_read_scope` rule that a removed member keeps reading the rows they authored; the shipped policy reads `scope_owner_id`, so the row is preserved and attributed but out of their read scope.
- **What changed — the test file only.** `pg_temp.as_server()` now clears the claims as well as the role, a new `pg_temp.as_user(uuid)` sets both, and every impersonation goes through one or the other, with each block that acts as a user naming that user explicitly. The removal block stages its own throwaway chamber with a throwaway owner and associate, so the refusal, the removal and the profile relink are judged against a clean seat. The read-scope assertions now expect the shipped rule, and the two checks that can be fooled report the status an RPC actually returned.
- **Proof.** `psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -v admin_id=… -v user_id=… -f supabase/tests/rpc_smoke_test.sql` against `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` printed `SMOKE OK: approve_payment, join_firm, ensure_firm and remove_firm_member behave as specified.` and exited 0, inside one transaction that rolls back and leaves no fixtures. `flutter analyze` clean, `python tool/record_version.py --check` OK. The plan (§ Revision 2.4, *Removing A Member*) and `docs/tasks/20_firm_management_and_delete_requests.md` already describe the removal rule and the scoped read policies, so per Rule 14 nothing new is recorded in them.
- **Resume point, next session.** The one remaining item from the ladder phase: the repo-wide "Part A / Part B" comment sweep.

Closing that properly needs a **signed update manifest checked against a key pinned in the app** — a key-generation decision for the user, not a code tweak — so it stands recorded as the phase's remaining gap rather than presented as met.

- **The request.** Build Phase 15, *Distribution* — two owed items and nothing else: **update authenticity** ("a signed release, or a checksum pinned in the app — so a tampered or unverifiable update is refused") and **the install path's docs** (the APK's download page, a stated owner, and install instructions that survive Android's unknown-sources prompt), client and docs only, **"Server: None"**, with the acceptance "a tampered or unverifiable release is refused rather than offered; the install path is documented and reachable without the app".
- **Four rulings taken before building (all recorded).** (1) The **download page is the project's GitHub releases page**, documented — no new site and no hosting, because a proper website comes later. (2) The install instructions are written in **English and Bengali**. (3) Authenticity is the plan's **first** option — **a signed release checked by the app** — rather than a fingerprint pinned in the app. (4) The **docs are corrected to the name GitHub actually publishes**, with no workflow change.
- **A finding that decided ruling 4.** The live release feed publishes the asset as `Legal.Case.Diary.v0.0.509-ARM64.apk`: the workflow sets a name with spaces and GitHub turns them into dots as it stores the file, so the plan's `Legal Case Diary v<version>-ARM64.apk` was a name no user ever downloads. Also worth knowing: the newest published release is **v0.0.509** while the app is at 0.0.541, so a download today is old — tagging and releasing is the user's step, and no tag was made in this pass.
- **The check, and where it lives.** In `MainActivity.kt`'s install handler, **before** the `FileProvider` lookup and any intent: the downloaded archive's signing certificate is read (`getPackageArchiveInfo` with `GET_SIGNING_CERTIFICATES` on API ≥ 28, the pre-28 `GET_SIGNATURES` below it — minSdk is 24, from the merged manifest), hashed with SHA-256, and compared with the certificate of **the app already installed**. A mismatch, an unreadable archive or a missing certificate answers `error("unverified_signature")` and dispatches nothing: no content URI, no per-resolver grant, no `startActivity`. It sits in Kotlin because reading a certificate is a platform API and the check has to be the same step that dispatches the intent, so the file cannot change between being verified and being handed over.
- **Why the app's own certificate is the anchor.** The installed app's signature is the identity Android itself enforces at install, so the check accepts exactly what the OS would accept, needs no value transcribed by hand, and cannot be broken by a keystore change that no code would see — the failure mode of a hard-coded fingerprint. The plan's alternative ("a checksum pinned in the app") was considered and declined for that reason, not overlooked.
- **The refusal the user reads.** The handoff returns a new three-way `ApkInstallOutcome` (`handedOff` / `unsupported` / `unverified`) instead of a bool, because *this device cannot install an update* would be an untrue explanation of a release that failed its authenticity check. `UpdateFlowError.unverifiedRelease` carries it to one new ARB key in both languages — *This update could not be verified, so it was not installed.* / *এই আপডেটটি যাচাই করা যায়নি, তাই ইনস্টল করা হয়নি।* — and it shows on both surfaces, the About card and the side menu's row, because they render the same body. A refusal does **not** clear the stored offer, so a refused release is never reported as the version in hand.
- **The install path's docs.** `README.md` gained **Installing The App (Android)**: the releases page as the download page, the owner named as the authority behind the releases (with the release page's *github-actions bot* publisher explained, kept honest after the audit), the asset name **as GitHub stores it**, and the numbered steps that survive Android's warning — including **Settings → Apps → Special access → Install unknown apps** and the older **Security → Unknown sources** spelling — then where later updates arrive (**Settings → About → Update → Check for update**, and the side menu's **Check for update** row), and the authenticity note in user words. Then the same content as **ইনস্টল করার নিয়ম (বাংলা)**. No website was built (ruling 1), so the readme is the download page until one exists.
- **Proof (the phase's own required test).** Eight new cases, and the accepted case kept working: `test/features/update_install_test.dart` gains the channel's refusal answered as a `PlatformException`, the same channel's normal handoff, the no-hook platform, and a different host refusal keeping its old meaning; the flow's refusal through the shared controller (`UpdateFlowController`) with real file IO, asserting the refusal state **and** that the stored offer still stands, plus the accepted handoff still clearing it; and two source assertions on the Kotlin — that the archive and the installed app are both read and hashed, that both API spellings exist, and that the refusal **precedes** the content URI and `startActivity`. `test/features/update_section_test.dart` gains the user-visible half: on the real Update screen, with the cache directory and the host's refusal mocked, the download runs, the refusal sentence appears, *you are on the latest version* does not, and the button returns to **Check for update**. **The new tests were proved to bite:** with the refusal mapped back to `unsupported`, exactly those three cases failed and the accepted case stayed green; the change was then reverted.

### 2026-10-18 — Firm mode Phase 13: a chamber refuses a restore, and what it may write when it does not — COMPLETE (0.0.538)

- **The request.** Build Phase 13: restore inside a chamber, where a restored row must be corrected by a tombstone and never overwrite a colleague's work — and the session's own note that a commit must carry the build, not tests or docs alone.
- **What the phase's ruling already said, and what the code did not do.** The user's ruling (plan, *Backup And Restore Inside A Chamber*; blueprint §6) has three parts: restore is barred whenever firm mode is on, the owner included, with a completely empty device as the only exception; the pull-only caches are never restored and a restored row's scope is settled into the current chamber while another chamber's file is refused; and attribution is not the restorer's to rewrite. The **bar** was the one part claimed as built, and it was not: the shipped 0.0.475 guard's only way through is **Delete Local & Cloud Data**, which the ruling rules out for a chamber — erasing a chamber's records from the server is not a choice a restore screen may make. The blueprint's "already built" note was corrected, and firm mode now gets a fence of its own.
- **The fence (client only, no migration).** `_restoreFromBackup` refuses before the folder scan and the picker when `firmModeProvider` is true and the diary holds user-authored data, through the new `showRestoreBarredInChamberDialog` (`backup_dialogs.dart`): the chamber sentence and one **Close**, no destructive action. The only restore firm mode allows is onto a device that holds nothing yet — a fresh install — which is where the full pull the ruling relies on runs over the restored rows and a tombstone from within the last 365 days corrects a stale restored row. Two ARB keys, en + bn, sentence case for the body.
- **The caches are never restored, through one shared scope.** `neverRestoredTables` (`profiles`, `firms`, `firm_members`) and `BackupRepository.restorableTables(fileTables)`, which the import walks **and** the screen's collision question asks, so the question and the write cannot disagree; a file holding only those tables now replaces nothing, asks nothing and counts nothing (the receipt no longer overstates what was written).
- **The scope is settled, not inherited.** New `settleRestoredScope` stamps this device's `firm_id` onto **every** restored row, and `stampRowOwnership` no longer writes `firm_id` at all — one column, one writer. It also closed a real hole: a file row with a **foreign** `firm_id` and **my** `user_id` used to pass the gate, and could then be pushed by nobody and read back by nobody, which is exactly the permanent local-only data the ruling forbids. `BackupOwnership.anotherFirm` / `BackupRestoreFailure.anotherFirm` now refuse it outright, whatever the owner column says, before the transaction opens, with their own sentence in both languages. `scope_owner_id` is cleared by construction rather than by code — it is a server column absent from the local schema and stripped from every push payload by `20261015110000` — and the doc comment names the one case that would change that.
- **Attribution is untouched, as before.** `user_id`, `created_by` and `last_modified_by` are written only where an owner cell names **nobody** (a hand-filled workbook); a colleague's row keeps its author, its attribution and its body and gains only the chamber it already belonged to.

The owner keeps both actions.

### 2026-10-17 — Firm mode Phase 11: the chamber goes and the ledger stays — COMPLETE (0.0.536)

- **The request.** Build Phase 11, dissolution: the owner removes every member, then dissolves; the chamber's rows become his own diary, its invites and its firm row go, his account returns to individual and his plan keeps running.
- **Server — one RPC, applied.** `supabase/migrations/20261017110000_firm_mode_dissolution.sql` adds `dissolve_firm()`: `SECURITY DEFINER`, **no arguments** (the firm is resolved from the caller, so it can never be aimed at another chamber), `execute` to `authenticated` only, applied to `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` and recorded by the applier. It locks the caller's `firms` row, counts the seats that are not the owner's and refuses with the count **before its first write**, retires the open invites, unscopes the eleven ledger tables in one loop (`firm_id` null, `scope_owner_id` the owner, tombstones included, the sync columns left to their triggers), clears `conflict_log`'s `firm_id` alone, relinks the owner's profile to `individual`, deletes the `firms` row (cascading memberships and invites) and pings `user:{owner}` as a `firm_members` change, which is the client's account refresh.
- **The finding §4.4 had not spelled out.** `conflict_log.firm_id` references `firms (id)` **without a cascade**, so a row left naming the chamber would make the `firms` delete fail outright. The dissolve clears that column and writes **no** scope owner — which is the ruling's own outcome, not a deviation: the author keeps their own merge diagnostics and the owner inherits none. The table has no `scope_owner_id` column to write, because it is not one of the eleven ledger tables.
- **The second finding: an unsynced edit would have been lost.** The client pushes before it pulls (`SyncService.syncNow` → `_drain(transport, pull: …)`), so a local edit still naming the chamber would be refused and rolled back the moment the chamber stopped existing. The action is therefore unavailable while `syncQueueEntriesProvider` holds anything and says so; after the dissolve the client refreshes the account and runs one pull, so the unscoped rows arrive locally without their old `firm_id`.
- **Client.** `FirmRepository.dissolveFirm()` with a count-carrying `DissolveRefusal` (worded through the one `failureText` entry point); the dissolve card at the foot of **Manage Associates**, blocked while the roster or the queue holds anything, naming the count still in the way, confirmed before it runs; and `ProfileRepository.refresh()` now clears the cached `firms` / `firm_members` rows when the profile stops naming a firm — a dissolve or a removal deletes those rows outright on the server, so no pull would ever tombstone them and the chamber would otherwise sit on the device for good.
- **Proof.** `supabase/tests/firm_mode_dissolution_test.sql`, one rolled-back run printing `DISSOLVE OK`: the refusal with its count and **nothing written** (no row, no invite, no profile), a member's `not_owner`, the real removal path emptying the roster, then the dissolve — the owner reads every row his members wrote while those accounts read none, attribution and contents and version and timestamps intact, `conflict_log` staying with its author, the pre-dissolve code answering `invalid_code`, the profile individual with name/expiry/tier untouched, and `delete_my_account()` answering `removed`. Client side, four new cases in `test/features/manage_associates_test.dart`: blocked with the count, dissolved after confirmation, a refusal from a newer roster showing its count and not claiming success, and a queued change blocking the action.
- **Checks, each run after the last edit it covers.** `flutter analyze` → `No issues found!` (exit 0); `flutter test` → **1835 passed** (exit 0); `dart run tool/generate_all_supabase_sql.dart --check` → clean; the SQL contract → `DISSOLVE OK` (exit 0) against the applied project. Live state verified by query and written into `supabase/README.md`: 26 tables with RLS on, 62 policies, 53 functions, 52 recorded versions (newest `20261017110000`), `authenticated` may execute `dissolve_firm()` and `anon` may not.
- **Records (rule 14).** §4.4's ruling was already in the blueprint, the plan and Task 20, so only as-built facts were added: §4.4's *As built (0.0.536)* paragraph (both findings), the Phase 11 section's status and *Built* field, the phase table row, §11's shipped list, the plan's *What Firm Mode Still Owes*, Task 20's *Phase 11 is built*, `supabase/README.md`'s test entry and live state, the generator's section label and group title, and the two contract tests that pin the migration count. No mockup is owed: Manage Associates has none (rule 9).

### 2026-10-17 — Firm mode Phase 10: a lapse caps writing at the tier's own allowance, and the free 50 wall stops standing in for it — COMPLETE (0.0.535)

- **The request.** Build Phase 10, the lapse allowance: a lapsed paid account keeps writing up to the allowance of the tier it last held — Pro 100, Firm 500, Firm Plus 1,000 cases, notes and case references — on the most recently updated rows, with everything beyond it readable but read-only, and the free account's 50-case wall kept only for an account that was never premium.
- **What the audit had found, and what this build closed.** The only gate in the app was `freeTierCaseLimit` (50) on the Add Case save path, so a lapsed Pro or Firm account would have been stopped at 50 rather than at its own allowance; and notes and case references had no ceiling at all. Both gaps are closed, and the chamber's tier is read on a member's device through the same derivation an individual uses, so a member's allowance is the chamber's.
- **No migration, and none needed.** The phase's own `Server` field says the entitlement gate on `push_changes` stays the boundary. It was already live, so this build is client-only: the server keeps refusing a lapsed account's pushes, and the device merely stops offering writes it would lose. No SQL was written, so `supabase/AllSupabaseSql.md` is unchanged and its drift check stays green.
- **The numbers now live on the tier, once.** `SubscriptionTier` (`lib/features/payments/data/payment_plans.dart`) carries a **case ceiling** and a **lapse allowance** per tier — free 50/0, pro 1,000/100, firm 2,500/500, firm_plus 6,000/1,000 — so the paywall, the gates and the tests read one row instead of retyping a figure; the free ceiling stays `freeTierCaseLimit`, so 50 is still written once.
- **One resolver, one shape, derived on demand.** `lib/features/settings/data/write_allowance.dart` turns a tier plus a premium flag into a `WriteAllowance`: premium unlimited, a genuinely free account with its add wall only, or a lapsed one with its ceiling and its writable id sets. The sets are the **most recently updated** live ids — `updated_at` descending with `id` as the tie-break, soft-deleted rows excluded — so the case in hand stays editable, deleting a writable row promotes the next one, and nothing is stored: renewal lifts the whole set at once. New DAO reads: `getMostRecentlyUpdatedIds` on cases, notes and references, and `getNonDeletedCount` on notes and references.
- **The tier read is the tier *in force*, not the stored key.** `lib/features/payments/data/plan_allowance.dart` repeats the server's `effective_tier` on the device, so a downgrade already under way counts from its own instant and a waiting pair that has not arrived leaves the stored tier standing. `allowanceTierProvider` and `writeAllowanceProvider` (`account_mode.dart`) resolve it once for the app and recompute when a case, note or reference changes; a premium or genuinely free account costs a single count and the stream then stops.
- **The gates, named.** Add Case's save path and the Quick Update dialog (`lib/shared/widgets/add_edit_case_sheet.dart`), where a lapsed account now goes to `AppRoutes.paywallFromLapse` and a genuinely free one stays on `paywallFromCaseLimit`; the note editor's save and pin, and the reference editor's save and pin — **the pins are gated deliberately**, because pinning writes `updated_at` and would otherwise pull a read-only row back inside the allowance; and the list and detail actions on the case screens, which explain the refusal instead of opening a form that would be refused on save.
- **What the user sees, and why nothing looks broken.** A lock on a read-only case card, table row, note card or reference card (`lib/shared/widgets/read_only_lock.dart`); one banner per list giving the editable and read-only counts with a **Renew** action, mounted once in the shared list shell (`lib/features/payments/presentation/lapse_allowance_ui.dart`); a **lapsed card** on the paywall behind `?reason=lapsed`, naming the allowance of the tier in force; each plan card printing its tier's own case ceiling; and a lapsed block on Subscription Details standing **in place of** the free-limitations block. Every refused write shows the same sentence and the same Renew route.
- **Two user-facing rulings this build needed, recorded.** (1) A lapsed account is named by its tier on the side menu and Subscription Details — *Pro — Lapsed* — rather than *Free*, because calling it Free contradicts the allowance it holds. (2) The paywall prints each plan's case ceiling instead of the withdrawn "unlimited cases" promise, since the ladder now has numbers; "Unlimited Cases" became "More Cases on Every Plan" in both languages.
- **One clause of §5.2 is not implemented, and the reason is a fact about the schema, not an omission.** *Children follow their parent* has **no site**: neither `notes` nor `case_references` carries a `case_id` (checked in `lib/database/tables/notes_table.dart` and `references_table.dart` — `userId`, `firmId` and their own columns only), so no note or reference is a child of a case. Nothing was invented for it; the note and reference ceilings apply in its place, and the rule becomes enforceable if such a link is ever added.
- **Tests.** New `test/features/lapse_allowance_test.dart` (8: the tier numbers, a waiting downgrade's own instant, an incomplete pair, premium, genuinely free, lapsed Pro, a deletion promoting the next row, the chamber tiers, the notes order) and `test/features/lapse_allowance_ui_test.dart` (6: the banner's counts and Renew action, its silence inside the allowance and for a premium account, the lock on a read-only card and its absence on a writable one, and the lapsed plan naming its tier). `paywall_screen_test.dart`, `subscription_details_screen_test.dart` and `app_navigation_drawer_test.dart` were updated for the new copy, and the paywall test now pins each tier's printed ceiling.
- **Checks, each run after the last edit it covers.** `flutter analyze` → `No issues found!` (exit 0); `flutter test` → **1831 passed** (exit 0). No Supabase statement was written, so no server proof was owed; `python tool/record_version.py --check` → clean at version **0.0.535**.

The mockups whose bodies moved (rule 9) now carry the banner and the read-only lock — the five case lists, Notes and Case Reference — and the paywall mockup carries the per-tier case ceilings and the revised benefits copy, with the lapsed card's own wording recorded beside the shared card rather than drawn, because the two states are exclusive and drawing both would show a screen the app never renders. **A closing sweep of `lib/` for stale "Part A / Part B" comments was left for the next session, exactly as the previous entry left it — it was not in this phase's scope.**

True for update, **false for insert**: `profiles` and `firms` each carried a *table-level* `insert` grant for `authenticated` and `anon`, a table-level grant reaches every column added afterwards, and both tables' insert policies let an account insert its **own** row (`id = auth.uid()`, `owner_id = auth.uid()`). The shipped form keys the **permission** rule on `auth.uid()` — the one thing both write doors have and a script does not — and the **scope** rule on the role, and the join-gate proof gained `pg_temp.as_owner()`, which clears the claim as well as the role.
