### 2026-10-02 — Online Sync: queued work outranks the plan, and the header counts it — COMPLETE

- **Request (the user's).** (1) Two pending syncs show correctly in Pending Sync but the Online Sync → Cases row said "Not synced". (2) Should the app header's sync/cloud button show a small red count of pending sync, so a user can see there is an issue?
- **(1) was a third real bug of mine, and the cause was the order of my own checks.** The row marker tested the **blocker first** (signed out / free plan / offline) and only then whether work was queued. So the moment anything was blocked, a queued change was reported as "Not synced" — telling the user nothing was waiting when two things were. Queued work is a **fact** independent of the plan or the connection, so `_markerIcon` / `_markerColor` / `_markerLabel` now check **waiting first**. The blockers only decide wording once there is genuinely nothing waiting, which is the only state "Not synced" actually describes. Pinned by `queued work outranks the blocker on every row` (a queued case edit on a free plan) and `a queued row is amber, never red`.
- **(2) is a good idea and is now done — but it needed one judgement.** The header **already** carries a red `sync_problem` badge, and it deliberately fires only for *blocked or conflicted* work: entries nothing will move on its own. Ordinary pending work is normal, so that badge stays quiet. Putting the count on the **sync button** is a different job — it answers "why has my edit not appeared on the other device yet?" — so it reads `syncQueuePendingCountProvider` rather than the attention provider. Two controls, two different facts, deliberately.
- **The button still syncs when tapped.** One control must do one thing, so the count is information only; where held work is *acted on* remains the Pending Sync entry on Online Sync. A red badge that navigated somewhere would have made the icon a lie. The count is suppressed while a sync is actually running, because a number beside a spinner reads as "stuck" when it is draining.
- **A rule-11 violation the suite caught, and I had introduced it.** `Badge.count` paints a **Latin** digit, so the Daily Cause List's own "counts use Bengali digits" test failed on my badge. It is now `AppDateUtils.formatDigits(pending, l.localeName)` like every other count in the app, and `the badge count uses the locale's digits` pins it.
- **Two sibling tests needed a judgement call, not a workaround.** `daily_cause_list_test.dart` and `upcoming_cases_test.dart` both seeded two cases — which queues a sync row each — then asserted `findsOneWidget` on "২". Both were **correctly** finding two counts: the court's, and now mine. Their actual intent ("no count is interpolated in Latin digits") is asserted by the second line, which stayed strict; only the over-tight "exactly one" became `findsNWidgets(2)`, with the reason recorded at each site.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1273 passed** (5 new); `arb_keys_test.dart` green. Version `0.0.357`.
- **Resume point:** no feature work open. Note for whoever adds more header badges: `Badge.count` is Latin-digit by default, and the case screens seed their data through `insertCase`, so any new count will collide with existing per-screen count assertions.

### 2026-10-02 — Online Sync: the redundant card gone, and two marker bugs fixed — COMPLETE

- **Request (the user's, five points).** Clearer subtitle; remove the "Premium Sync Is Active Across Your Devices" card as redundant; a synced case wrongly reads "Not synced"; empty Notes and References read "Not synced" **in green**, which should be red; and rename Sync Status to **Pending Sync**, moved to the very bottom after References.
- **Points 3 and 4 were real bugs I shipped yesterday, not wording.** The row marker used a single `queued > 0 ? … : notSynced` ternary with `AppColors.success` on the empty branch, so an entity with nothing waiting always read "Not synced" — in **green**, next to a Sync Now button that was itself disabled. A green "Not synced" is self-contradictory: it says the thing is broken and the thing is fine in the same breath. The row now derives one marker from **two** facts: whether it has work waiting, and **whether it can reach the account at all** (`_syncBlockerOf(ref)`, the same blocker rule the status card uses, so the two cannot disagree). Three states, one per real condition: **Synced** (green, nothing waiting and sync is possible), **"N Waiting"** (muted, work is queued), **"Not synced"** (red, blocked — with "Sign in to sync" when the blocker is that nobody is signed in, because that wording tells the user what to do and "Not synced" does not). A free account therefore never claims Synced for something that was never sent.
- **The account card is deleted, not hidden.** The status card still carries the four blockers, so "what state is sync in" survives; what is gone is the second copy of the account, which Settings > Manage Account already owns. Its now-dead locals (`identity`, `premium`, `online`) and its `profile_name_store` import went with it, rather than being left as unused reads.
- **Pending Sync sits last, and has its own label.** It keeps opening the Sync Status screen but is titled `settingsOnlineSync_pendingSyncTitle` rather than reusing `syncStatus_title`, which **names that screen's own header** — reusing the key would have renamed the Sync Status screen and the header badge tooltip with it.
- **The subtitle now says what actually happens**: records are kept up to date on this device and sent to the account when you are on Premium. The old "Manage your real-time data sync" promised real-time, which this engine does not do.
- **Two of the three new ARB states are regression tests**, not just new coverage: `a row that cannot sync is red, never green` reads the rendered `Text.style.color` and asserts `AppColors.error`, and `a synced row is green` asserts `AppColors.success`. `Pending Sync is the last thing on the screen` compares `getTopLeft` against References so the ordering cannot silently move back.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1268 passed** (13 in this screen's suite); `arb_keys_test.dart` green. Version `0.0.356`.

### 2026-10-02 — Online Sync: the real account, plan and engine — COMPLETE

- **Request (the user's).** "I'm currently logged in the app but in the screen it says I'm not", and to wire the screen's options properly.
- **The cause was that the screen was never finished.** `OnlineSyncScreen` was still the **Part A stub**: a `StatelessWidget` account card that rendered `settingsOnlineSync_notSignedIn` unconditionally, a hard-coded "Action Required / Last Sync: Never", and a Sync Now button that only showed a snackbar. Every string came from the mockup's *signed-out* frame. It was never wired to the Part B engine, and **no test referenced it at all** — which is exactly how it survived while Tasks 17–19 built the whole sync engine underneath it.
- **The account card now reads the account.** The same three-source name fallback Manage Account uses (this device's saved name → the session's → the server's cached profile), so a signed-in premium user sees their own name and "Premium Sync Is Active"; the signed-out wording is now reached only when there genuinely is no identity.
- **The plan decides whether sync can run, and the button says so.** `premiumAccessProvider` and `isOnlineProvider` feed a small blocker, so the button is **disabled with a reason** rather than firing a no-op: free plan → "Premium Is Required To Sync Across Devices.", offline → "No Connection…", signed out → "Sign In To Sync…". This matters because `SyncService` enforces all three itself by **silently returning** — a button that appears to work while doing nothing is worse than one that explains itself.
- **Sync Now really syncs.** It calls `syncNow(force: true, pull: true)` and then reads `consecutiveFailures` back off the published health, because `syncNow` returns `void` and signals failure through health and notices rather than a result value.
- **The status card is now the engine's.** Real last-sync via `syncLastSuccessProvider` (this **device's** value, the one the recovery lock also reads), the attention count for blocked/conflicted work, the pending-upload count, and health (syncing/paused). The pill is `Up To Date` when there is nothing to say, and `Action Required` when something cannot resolve itself.
- **What the screen still does not claim.** There is **no per-entity "synced" flag anywhere in this app** — the engine stores a device-level last-sync and per-table pull cursors, neither of which is per-entity sync state. So an entity row shows its count and whether it has work **waiting to send** (derived from real `sync_queue` rows by `entity_type`), and is never marked "Synced". This is stated in the file's header so a later reader does not mistake the omission for an oversight.
- **A test suite now exists** — `test/features/online_sync_screen_test.dart`, 10 tests, which the screen never had. Three assertions failed on first run and each was a real finding, not a test bug: "Not signed in" legitimately renders **twice** (account card + status pill, one answering "who" and one answering "what state"), the entity rows needed a tall viewport because a lazy `ListView` never builds an off-screen row, and the never-synced and just-synced cases needed to be separate tests rather than two pumps of one.
- **A careless detour, corrected.** A reorder script I wrote to sync the two ARB files' key order reserialized the whole Bengali file — 326 insertions of unrelated metadata reformatting. I reverted it and hand-moved the four misplaced keys instead, so the final diff is **68 insertions and nothing else**. `arb_keys_test.dart` passes.
- **The mockup is left as-is, deliberately.** `settings_onlineSync/code.html` draws the **signed-out** state, and the screen still renders that state identically, so the design reference still holds. Nothing to correct until the mockups are refreshed.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1265 passed** (10 new). Version `0.0.355`.

### 2026-10-02 — Premium: the paywall insets its own status bar — COMPLETE

- **Request (the user's).** The Premium screen does not show the phone's status bar the way other screens do.
- **Cause.** The paywall is a **top-level route** (`app_router.dart`, outside `ShellRoute`), so the shell's `SafeArea(top: true, bottom: false)` never reaches it. Without that inset the `Scaffold` paints its app bar from y=0, so the clock and status icons land on the app bar's white instead of on the app's own black status-bar band — the one screen where they disappear.
- **The fix is the shell's own pattern, not a new one.** `SafeArea(top: true, bottom: false)` wrapping the whole `Scaffold`, exactly as `AppShellRoot` does. Verified by measurement, not by eye: with a simulated 90 px status bar the app bar now starts at `top = 90` and keeps its own 56 px height, matching `SettingsSubPageModal` and the shell screens. A first attempt that wrapped only the `body` was wrong — the app bar sits outside the body, so it changed nothing and the probe numbers were identical; the `SafeArea` has to be an ancestor of the `Scaffold`.
- **Pinned by test.** New `leaves the phone status bar visible above its app bar` asserts the app bar's `top` equals the injected status-bar height and its height is below it. `pumpPaywall` gained a `statusBarHeight` parameter defaulting to 0, so the existing assertions are unaffected.
- **Not changed:** `checkout_screen.dart` has the same structure and the same latent problem, but it was out of scope. Flagged below.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1246 passed**. Version `0.0.353`.

### 2026-10-01 — Auth E-mail links open the app, and Google sign-in checks the network first — COMPLETE

- **Request (two points, both the user's).** (1) *All this time* the Google sign-in failure had been **internet connectivity** — the phone was on a Wi-Fi network with no internet, and turning on mobile data fixed it — so why could the tooling not tell? (2) When Supabase mails a sign-up confirmation or a password-reset link, tapping it opens `localhost:3000` instead of the app.
- **Why the failure was invisible, stated plainly (no defensiveness).** The old `mapAuthFailure` folded every on-device Google `canceled` into `AuthFailureKind.cancelled`, and both screens deliberately render `cancelled` as **no message at all** — so a dead network and a real dismissal produced byte-identical behaviour. The one surviving signal, GMS `[16] Account reauth failed.`, is raised for *both* a missing certificate and a reauth request that never reached Google, and the plugin's README says it cannot distinguish them; reading it as leaning configuration was **over-confident**. The previous "cause: the signing certificate is not registered" conclusion is therefore **corrected below**: registering the debug/release/Play certificates remains a genuine prerequisite for Google sign-in on release builds, but it was never proven to be this cause.
- **Even today's code could not have told, and that is the real gap.** The project's own `ConnectivityMonitor` answers the **link, not the internet** on purpose — a Wi-Fi network with no uplink reports "connected" — so `connectivity_plus` would have said the phone was online. Only an actual request that has to complete can see it.
- **What changed — the links (the user's choice was the real deep link, not a dashboard-only fix).** `SupabaseConfig.authRedirectUrl` = `com.legalcasediary.app://login-callback`, passed as `emailRedirectTo` by `signUpIndividual` and as `redirectTo` by `sendPasswordRecoveryCode`, because Supabase otherwise falls back to the project **Site URL** — whose dashboard default is `http://localhost:3000`, exactly the reported symptom. `android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` claims the scheme with its own `<intent-filter>` **and** sets `flutter_deeplinking_enabled=false`, which the `app_links` docs require from Flutter 3.24 or the engine consumes the URI first. A verified recovery link signs the user in as a side effect, so `AuthSessionEvent` gained `passwordRecovery` (from `AuthChangeEvent.passwordRecovery`), `AuthState` gained the matching flag exposed as `passwordRecoveryPendingProvider`, the router gained one rule holding the user on the reset screen until the new password is set, and that screen asks for the password alone (no address, no code) and hides the way back to Login. **The emailed-code flow is unchanged and stays primary** — the earlier "the code, not a deep link, brings the user back" design note is superseded only by *adding* the link as a second way in.
- **What changed — the network probe.** `probeSupabaseReachable` is a four-second request to the project URL, injectable for tests, run by `signInWithGoogle` **before** the account sheet opens; a failure raises `AuthFailureKind.network`, whose existing copy is *"No Connection. Check Your Internet And Try Again."* The cheap `connectivity_plus` alternative was offered and rejected in the plan discussion for exactly the reason above: it cannot see dead Wi-Fi.
- **Records (rule 14 — both changes are absent from the plan).** A long *Auth E-mail Links Return To The App, And Google Sign-In Checks The Network First* bullet in the plan's Resolved Design Clarifications and a matching Addendum bullet in `docs/tasks/17_auth_profiles_and_firm_onboarding.md`. Runbook `docs/google_oauth_setup.md` gained **§10.1** (the two dashboard values, what each link does, the `adb` deep-link test), two symptom rows, and four checklist items; `README.md` gained an *Auth E-mail Links* section and a "check the network first" bullet.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1244 passed** (1241 + 3: the link-path screen test and two probe tests); `record_version.py --check` OK; `generate_all_supabase_sql.dart --check` OK (no SQL this phase). Version `0.0.348`.
- **Still the user's to do (dashboard-only, unreadable from this machine).** Add `com.legalcasediary.app://login-callback` to **Authentication → URL Configuration → Redirect URLs**; point **Site URL** at a real page; keep `{{ .Token }}` in the Reset Password template; then prove both with a real sign-up mail on the device.
- **Resume point:** no feature work open. The definitive proof of Google sign-in is still a successful run leaving an `id_token` grant in the Auth logs — and the next offline attempt should now say *No Connection* rather than nothing.

### 2026-10-01 — Google sign-in: the failure is now reported instead of swallowed — COMPLETE

- **Request.** Google sign-in worked at sign-up but later stopped: after picking the account in the sheet the app simply stayed on the login screen.
- **Diagnosis first (the user's ruling), and it was conclusive.** An instrumented build printed `I/flutter: Google sign-in failed: GoogleSignInException(code GoogleSignInExceptionCode.canceled, [16] Account reauth failed., null)` — Android Credential Manager returns `[16]` → `GetCredentialCancellationException` → plugin `CANCELED` → Dart `canceled`. The old `mapAuthFailure` folded that into `AuthFailureKind.cancelled`, and both screens deliberately render `cancelled` as **no message**, so a real failure was indistinguishable from the user closing the sheet. The plugin's own README states the two cases are indistinguishable by design and lists the causes (missing/incorrect signing SHA, wrong package name, wrong `serverClientId`). The server is innocent: 24h of Auth logs on `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` contain **no `id_token` grant** at all — the app aborts on-device before any Supabase call — and the single user (`asad.msnd@gmail.com`) signed up with Google successfully, so the Supabase provider config is fine. **Cause: the signing certificate is not registered in Google Cloud.** — *Corrected 2026-10-01: the user's later evidence showed the real cause was a **Wi-Fi network with no internet**, fixed by switching to mobile data (see the entry above). The certificate registration remains a prerequisite for Google sign-in on release builds, but it was never proven to be this cause, and `[16]` is consistent with both.*
- **App-side fix (chosen from the offered options).** New `AuthFailureKind.googleSignInFailed` with EN/BN copy (“Google Sign-In Could Not Complete. Please Try Again.” / Bengali in `app_en.arb`/`app_bn.arb`), raised when the cancellation carries a GMS code (matched as `^\[\d+\]` on the exception description) or when the code is `clientConfigurationError`/`providerConfigurationError`; a description-less `canceled` stays silent, which the pre-existing test still pins. The screens needed no change — they already show a banner for every kind except `cancelled`.
- **The temporary `debugPrint` was removed** once it had served its purpose; the diagnostic is now a permanent, tested mapping rather than a log line.
- **Server-side work is the user's, and is documented.** `README.md` gained *Google Sign-In Setup and Troubleshooting*: the debug and release SHA-1/SHA-256 fingerprints, both Android OAuth clients in the same project as the Web client, Play's own app-signing certificate (Play re-signs uploads), the package name `com.legalcasediary.app`, the consent-screen *Test users* rule while unpublished, and the reproducible command. The user chose to register **both** debug and release fingerprints.
- **The category label is the user's call, not the mockup's (corrected).** I first read `settingsCourtNamesSteps_catDistrictSessions` = “Sessions (Criminal)” as an accidental regression from commit `9172339` and restored the mockup's “District & Sessions (Criminal)”. **The user then stated the rename was deliberate and set the value to “Sessions Courts (Criminal)”.** The ARB key is now off-limits to me. Its consequences were carried through instead: `court_names_steps_test.dart`'s expected card label, the `settings_courtNamesSteps` mockup card and the category list in `docs/tasks/12_settings_screens.md` now all read “Sessions Courts (Criminal)”, and `flutter gen-l10n` was rerun so the generated localizations agree. The Bengali ARB was **left untouched** (still “জেলা ও দায়রা (ফৌজদারি)”) — rewriting Bengali copy is the user's call, and it is flagged below. The v0.0.341 history line's claim that the label was *restored to match its mockup* stands as recorded but is superseded by `0.0.342`.
- **Open question, deliberately not guessed:** EN and BN currently name different categories for this key. The Bengali wording still says District & Sessions.
- **Records (rule 14 — absent from the plan).** A *A Google Failure Is Reported, Not Swallowed* bullet added to the plan's Resolved Design Clarifications and a matching bullet in `docs/tasks/17_auth_profiles_and_firm_onboarding.md`'s Addendum.
- **Setup runbook written for a novice (the user's request).** `docs/google_oauth_setup.md` walks the whole console: the three-party mental model (app certificate → Android client, `serverClientId` → Web client, consent screen → who may sign in); the exact project number, package name, Web client ID and both SHA-1s; the mandatory Branding/Audience registration and the *Testing* → **Test users** rule; scopes (`openid` added by hand, nothing sensitive); one Android client per certificate — debug, release, and **Play's own app-signing certificate**, because Play re-signs uploads; the iOS client as a later step; checking the Web client's redirect URI against Supabase's callback; the Supabase Google provider step (Web client ID first, secret only there); then ordered pass/fail verification, a symptom → cause table, and a tick-box checklist. Grounded in Google's *Manage OAuth Clients* help page (which confirms the SHA-1 only, and the 5-minutes-to-a-few-hours propagation) and Supabase's *Sign in with Google* guide (Web-first comma-separated client IDs). Linked from `README.md`.
- **Second correction: the Authorized domain must be the full project host, not `supabase.co` (v0.0.347).** `supabase.co` is rejected with *"Invalid domain: must be a top private domain"* — correctly, because `supabase.co` (like `supabase.in` and `supabase.net`) is listed in the **private section of the Public Suffix List**, so it is a public suffix and not a registrable domain. The registrable (top private) domain of the callback host `https://lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau.supabase.co/auth/v1/callback` is therefore **`lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau.supabase.co`**, which is what goes in box 1 — matching the community reports that use the Supabase project URL itself as the authorized domain. §5.3 and the §14 checklist updated.
- **The user's Google Sites pages are excluded from the Branding page, with the reason and the upgrade path recorded (v0.0.346).** The user has a Google Site (`https://sites.google.com/view/legal-case-diary/{about,privacy-policy,terms-of-service}`) and asked whether to use it as the App domain. Answer: **no**, because `sites.google.com` is **Google's** domain — *App Homepage* help page: *"Your homepage and privacy policy should not be hosted on a third-party platform where you can't verify that you own your subdomain. For example: Google Sites, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter."* The homepage must be *"hosted on a verified domain you own"*, and `sites.google.com` cannot be added to *Authorized domains* either. The pages stay useful for the Play Console listing (which does accept them) and in-app links. **Upgrade path documented:** buy a domain, connect it to the same Google Site (Settings → Custom domains), verify it in Search Console, then add it as an authorized domain and point the three App-domain fields at it — a Google Site served on your own verified domain is acceptable; it is the `sites.google.com` host Google rejects. New §5.2.1.
- **Correction to the same runbook: Authorized domains is mandatory, and the correct value is `supabase.co` (v0.0.345).** My first pass told the user to leave the Authorized-domains boxes empty; the console refuses that with *"Invalid domain: must not be empty"*. Google's *Manage OAuth App Branding* help page is explicit that *all* domains used on the Branding page **or in an OAuth client's configuration** must be pre-registered, and this project's only such domain is the Supabase callback host `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau.supabase.co` — so its top private domain `supabase.co` goes in box 1 (the bare domain, no protocol or path; the full project host is the fallback if the form refuses it). Ownership is not checked at entry time; it matters only at verification, where the established Supabase answer is to confirm your own domain and tell Google the Supabase entry is the third-party auth provider, keeping your own domain first. If the user later owns a domain it goes in as a second entry, first in the list, and the §5.2 App-domain links then point at it. §5.3 and the §14 checklist both corrected.
- **The runbook's Branding section was too thin (user's follow-up, fixed).** §5 now walks every field the console shows: the top fields (app name, support email, developer contact email — the last is **not** user-visible), the *App domain* block (**Application home page** / **privacy policy link** / **terms of service link** — all left blank while in Testing, required only for verification, and never pointed at a URL the developer does not own), and the *Authorized domains* block (all three boxes blank for this app: a domain there must be **owned** and ownership-verified, so `supabase.co` must **not** be added; the Supabase callback is a redirect URI on the Web client, a different page and rule, and the app signs in natively without ever visiting it). Added a matching blank-fields tick to the §14 checklist. Version `0.0.344`.
- **Verification.** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1241 passed** (1239 + 2 new classification tests); `court_names_steps_test.dart` green under the new label; `record_version.py --check` OK. ### 2026-10-01 — Build wrapper: credentials injected for debug and release — COMPLETE

- **Request.** Let the credentials be injected during a debug/release build without having to remember the flag each time, while keeping them out of the repository.
- **What it is.** `tool/flutter_with_env.dart` forwards every argument to `flutter` and appends `--dart-define-from-file=<project root>/env.json`, so both `run` (debug) and `build` (release) go through one path. It resolves `env.json` from the project root (usable from any working directory), uses `flutter.bat` on Windows so the executable resolves reliably, and **exits non-zero with a clear message when `env.json` is missing**, so a release can no longer ship silently offline. The constants are compile-time, so this is genuinely build-time injection — there is no runtime fetch; a hot restart still will not pick up a changed file, only a rebuild will.
- **Usage.** `dart run tool/flutter_with_env.dart run -d <device>` and `dart run tool/flutter_with_env.dart build apk --release`. Documented in `README.md` alongside the existing raw-flag commands.
- **Records (rule 14 — absent from the plan).** A **Build Credentials Seam** bullet was added to the plan's Resolved Design Clarifications, the same follow-up noted in `docs/tasks/17_auth_profiles_and_firm_onboarding.md`'s Addendum, and `README.md` updated.
- **Verification.** `dart analyze tool/flutter_with_env.dart` clean and `flutter analyze` clean; the wrapper ran a real `flutter test test/l10n/arb_keys_test.dart` (4 passed) proving the flag is forwarded, and the no-args path printed usage with exit 2. Version `0.0.340`.
- **Resume point:** no feature work open. The four-plan Premium change (v0.0.339) and this wrapper are both uncommitted.

### 2026-10-01 — Task 21 Phase 4: grace, expiry and the upgrade — COMPLETE

- **The banner is derived, non-dismissible, and silent for a free account.** `subscription_banner.dart` computes one of four states from the cached expiry and the recorded clock offset (`resolveSubscriptionBanner`, pure and unit-tested): **none** (active, or never subscribed — no expiry means no nag), **grace** (past expiry but inside 48h: *"Your subscription expired. Renew to avoid losing sync access."*), **expiredOwner** (*"Your premium subscription has ended. Renew your subscription to restore sync."*), and **expiredAssociate** (*"Your firm's premium subscription has ended. Contact your firm owner to renew."*) — the associate/owner split is `firmMember && role != owner`, because an associate's entitlement is the owner's. It is deliberately **not** dismissible: a renewal warning the user swiped away is one they never saw. Mounted in the same two hosts the conflict banner uses (`AppShellRoot` and `CasesScreenModal`), above the notice and conflict strips; it renders `SizedBox.shrink()` when all is well. Since the sync gate already refuses to run below the derived entitlement, "sync disabled immediately after grace, no data deleted" needed no new code — this is the visible half.
- **Activation detection is durable, because the upgrade can happen while the app is closed.** `SubscriptionActivation.observe(premium)` stores the last observed entitlement per account (`subscription_was_premium_<userId>`) and runs `SyncService.runBacklogPush()` exactly when a stored `false` becomes `true`. A missing value is *no prior state* — a first-ever launch stores the value and never pushes, so a new install cannot fire a backlog pass — and a stored `false` that reads `true` on the next launch is the approval landing during the profile refresh (Task 18's backlog pass had no production caller until now). Wired into `sync_trigger_scope.dart`'s existing `premiumAccessProvider` listener, so the runtime transition and the launch/resume refresh both flow through one path. **A Broadcast ping is not used and cannot be:** `profiles`/`payment_submissions` carry no row trigger, so the plan's "Broadcast ping **or** profile refresh" is satisfied by the refresh.
- **Manage Account now shows the plan and the expiry, in `DD/MM/YYYY`.** Behind Subscription Details (the existing sheet), a **Plan** row names the paid plan from the latest **approved** submission and a dash when there is none (the Subscription row already says Free/Premium, so a repeated tier word would be noise), and an **Expiry** row renders the expiry in the active locale's `DD/MM/YYYY` (or a dash). The sheet body was already made scrollable in Phase 2 for the history.
- **Tests:** 15 new — 6 in `test/features/subscription_banner_test.dart` (active/none, no-expiry, grace, past-grace owner, past-grace associate + owner, and the clock-skew flip) plus 4 widget cases (each message rendered, nothing when active) and 5 in `test/features/subscription_activation_test.dart` (first launch stores without pushing, a stored false→true pushes once, an upgrade across a restart is detected, a lapse and re-upgrade pushes again, and state is per account). One regression surfaced and was fixed: the new Plan row duplicated the tier word already in the Subscription row, so two `manage_account_test.dart` expectations matched twice; the Plan row now shows a dash without an approved submission, and the suite is green. Full `flutter test` **1239 passed** (1198 → 1239); `flutter analyze` clean; ledger `--check` clean; `python tool/record_version.py --check` clean. Version `0.0.336`.

### 2026-10-01 — Task 21 Phase 2: the checkout submits, remembers and limits — COMPLETE

- **One write path, and it never touches the server's authority.** `SupabasePaymentRepository.submit` INSERTs one own `payment_submissions` row (RLS: `user_id = auth.uid()`) and deliberately omits `submitted_at` — the server's `BEFORE INSERT` trigger assigns it, so a client value is never sent. `status` stays the server default. A `PostgrestException` is mapped to a typed `PaymentSubmitException` — the trigger's `payment_submission_limit_reached` becomes `limitReached`, a `23505` becomes `duplicateTransaction`, anything else `other`; anything non-PostgREST is `network`. `UnavailablePaymentRepository` reports every submit as `network` for a no-backend build rather than pretending a queue.
- **The draft is the point: it survives a failure and is cleared only on a confirmed success.** `PaymentDraftNotifier` keys `payment_draft_<userId>` in `SharedPreferences` (`PaymentDraft` = plan, method, phone, TrxID), saves on every keystroke through the two controller listeners, and restores in `initState`. The view model clears it and records the local stamp **only after** the repository returned without throwing; a refusal leaves both untouched. Per-user keys mean one account's half-typed TrxID never appears in another's form (Addendum: checkout drafts are never firm-shared).
- **The local 3-per-24h check is UX, and the code says so.** `PaymentSubmissionLogNotifier` keeps accepted-submission epoch stamps per user; `localSubmissionsInWindow`/`isLocallyRateLimited` are pure so the rule is unit-tested. The screen checks them before submitting to save a round trip, and the server's trigger remains authoritative — a `limitReached` refusal is worded with the same friendly sentence. A reached local limit shows *"You've reached today's submission limit. Please try again tomorrow."*; a duplicate TrxID gets its own sentence.
- **The view model owns the phase, the screen owns the wording.** `PaymentViewModel.submit` walks `idle → submitting → success/failure`, refuses an unknown plan and a signed-out caller without a request, and invalidates `myPaymentSubmissionsProvider` on success so the history refreshes. Failure kinds map to the task's exact sentences: *"Submission failed. Tap Retry."* for network/other, the limit sentence for the trigger, and a sign-in sentence when nobody is signed in.
- **History lives behind Subscription Details in Manage Account.** Phase 2 item 4, placement confirmed with the user: the sheet gained a `Payment History` section over `myPaymentSubmissionsProvider` (own rows only under RLS), each row showing the plan, the amount in the active locale's digits, a status pill (pending/approved/rejected) and the reviewer's `admin_notes`. The sheet body became scrollable so an arbitrarily long history cannot overflow it; the mockup-bound Manage Account list needed no new row.

### 2026-10-01 — Task 20 follow-up: RLS refuses the write the RPC already refuses — COMPLETE

- **The residual the audit flagged is closed at the policy layer, by the user's choice of scope.** `0.0.330` hardened `sync_can_write`, which is the path the *app* uses. The table policies still said `user_id = auth.uid()` on a firm-scoped row, and Supabase grants `authenticated` table-level write privileges by default, so the same removed associate could PATCH their authored firm rows straight through PostgREST — with the RPC, its version check and its receipts never involved. Worse than an edit: `cases_update_scoped`'s `with check` asked only that the NEW row keep `user_id = auth.uid()`, so a removed member could detach a firm record by nulling `firm_id`. Asked how far to go, the user chose **policies only, no grant changes**, so the direct path is now refused *by policy* rather than made unreachable by revoked privileges.
- **`20260930220000_rls_firm_membership.sql` states the same rule as the closure, in the same places.** Every INSERT and UPDATE policy that trusts authorship now requires the row to be personal (`firm_id is null`) or still the caller's firm (`firm_id is not distinct from public.current_firm_id()`) — the ten tables that share one policy shape (`cases`, `case_history`, `notes`, `case_references`, the six reference tables) are handled by one loop so their spellings cannot drift, with `conflict_log` (own rows only, no `can_edit_firm` disjunct) and `delete_requests` (whose author column is `requested_by`) written out by hand. `using` and `with check` say the same thing, which is what stops a row being updated *into* a state its writer could not have created. `can_edit_firm` / `can_delete_firm` are unchanged, so teammates and reviewers keep their access, and a `firm_id`-less personal row is untouched — that is the individual diary AGENTS rule 3 protects.
- **Two limits, both deliberate and both recorded in the migration.** SELECT policies are left alone: they compare the row's firm to the caller's with a plain equality, and a NULL on either side is not true, so a caller with no firm already reads nothing from a firm row — `is not distinct from` would be equivalent there, and rewriting a read policy for no behavioural gain is risk without reward. Table privileges are left alone by the user's decision; the migration says so plainly, including that revoking them would have closed the direct path too.
- **Applied live and proven on `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau`, in both directions.** Before the apply, `has_table_privilege('authenticated','public.cases','UPDATE')` was true and the with-check read `(user_id = auth.uid()) OR can_edit_firm(firm_id)`; after it, `pg_get_expr` shows the membership condition on `cases`, `courts`, `conflict_log` and `delete_requests`, with the privilege deliberately unchanged. `supabase/tests/push_changes_smoke_test.sql` gained a rolled-back section that stops using the RPC and acts as the `authenticated` role instead, so RLS is evaluated rather than the owner's privileges: the removed member's direct PATCH of the firm row they authored updates **zero** rows, a direct INSERT into the firm fails the `WITH CHECK` (an error rather than an empty result, so both shapes are pinned), their pending firm request is likewise out of reach — and the owner's own direct edit still lands, so a policy that refused everything could not pass the section. Then the whole smoke run printed `SMOKE OK`, and the new assertions were proven to bite by inverting one on a scratch copy, which failed with exactly that message.
- **Guards:** `test/supabase/schema_contract_test.dart` gained a structural check on the new file (the membership comparison present, no NULL-prone equality, all ten loop tables named, `conflict_log` and `delete_requests` present, the reviewer disjuncts intact, no `for select`), and the two hard-coded migration counts moved 26 → 27 with `versions.last` now `20260930220000`.
- **Tests:** full `flutter test` **1198 passed** (1197 → 1198); `test/supabase/` 78 passed; `flutter analyze` clean; ledger `--check` clean at 27 migrations / 585 KB; `python tool/record_version.py --check` clean. Version `0.0.332`.
- **Resume point:** Task 20 is now closed on both sides of the membership rule, so the next step is the task file's acceptance checklist (phases + Addendum) or Task 21 directly — whose Phase 1 opens with the two `[Design-deferred]` screens (Paywall, Checkout) that need layout confirmation before any code, and whose Phase 4 end-to-end approval test still faces the one-live-account constraint that kept `rpc_smoke_test.sql` from running.

### 2026-10-01 — Task 20 Phase 3 item 3 closed: the requester can edit and withdraw their own pending request — COMPLETE

- **The last audit gap was a missing surface, not a missing rule.** Phase 3 item 3 ("the requester can edit/cancel their own pending request") had been satisfied only at the data layer since `0.0.326` — `refreshSnapshot`, `cancel` and `watchMine` all existed and worked — but the requester's list rows were deliberately non-interactive (`onTap: null`), so there was no way to reach either writer. This change adds the surface and nothing else; no repository, DAO, table or server code changed.
- **"Edit" was the one genuinely ambiguous word, so it was put to the user before any code.** A `delete_requests` row carries no free text: its editable content is the `entity_snapshot` of the target and the `target_base_version` it was observed at. The user chose **re-take the snapshot** (over "refresh only when the record actually changed" and over "withdraw and re-raise a fresh request"), and chose the **row-tap action sheet** as the surface (over inline buttons and a trailing overflow menu) — both the smaller and the more conventional option, matching Case History's action sheet and Manage Associates' member sheet.
- **Edit re-reads the record through its own feature's repository, not off a screen.** `DeleteRequestsViewModel.refreshSnapshot(id)` loads the request, refuses anything that is not still `pending`, resolves the target by `entity_type`/`entity_id` through `caseRepositoryProvider` / `caseHistoryRepositoryProvider` / `notesRepositoryProvider` / `referenceRepositoryProvider` (the same rows the original snapshot was taken from, and the same four kinds a request can name), and then re-uses the existing `deleteRequestSnapshot` / `deletionBaseVersion` helpers so the refreshed payload and version rule cannot drift from the ones the request was first raised with. A target this device no longer holds — deleted, or authored elsewhere and never pulled — is a **null the caller must handle**, and the screen says so rather than reporting a refresh that never happened. `cancel(id)` is the same shape around the existing `LocalDeleteRequestsRepository.cancel`, so the soft-delete and its queued `delete` were already correct and untouched.
- **One row, two states, one sheet.** In `delete_requests_screen.dart`, a **pending** row of `myDeleteRequestsProvider` now opens a bottom sheet with **Edit Request** and a red **Withdraw Request**; a **decided** row stays a plain, unkeyed container showing its status pill. The row widget gained `showStatusChip` rather than deriving the trailing affordance from `onTap`, because the requester's list carries both pending and decided rows — losing the pill on a pending row would have made it unreadable — while the reviewer's queue, where everything is pending by definition, keeps rendering exactly as before. Withdrawal is confirmed first (an edit can be repeated, a withdrawal cannot) and the confirmation says out loud that the record is *not* deleted and the request leaves the reviewers' queue. Both actions catch a refused or failed write and report "nothing changed", which is the honest wording for a request that was decided on another device.
- **Eight new ARB keys, appended in one block to `@@_section_deleteRequests`** in `app_en.arb` and `app_bn.arb`, key-for-key and order-for-order (995 keys each), Title Case in English, Bengali hand-written, `flutter gen-l10n` re-run. Both files' CRLF endings were preserved by the editor.
- **Tests:** 4 new in `test/features/delete_request_review_test.dart` — a pending row offers both actions, a decided row is not even a gesture target, editing re-takes the snapshot (the note's new title and `version` 7 land in the stored row while `status` stays `pending`, with exactly one queued `update` whose `changed_fields` name `entity_snapshot`/`target_base_version`/`updated_at`), and withdrawing writes nothing until the confirmation is tapped, then soft-deletes the row and queues exactly one `delete` carrying `is_deleted: true`. Full `flutter test` **1197 passed** (1193 → 1197); `flutter analyze` clean; ledger `--check` clean (no SQL this phase); `python tool/record_version.py --check` clean. Version `0.0.331`.
- **Resume point:** the requester side is now complete, so Task 20's remaining work is the task file's **acceptance checklist run item by item** (including the Rev 2.3/2.4 Alignment Addendum), plus the user's outstanding rulings on the previously flagged interpretive choices: the pending-deletion marker sits on the queue row rather than the record; the reviewer sees the requester's name best-effort and `deleteRequests_unknownRequester` otherwise; a queued-but-unsent review is not separately marked; and the Settings dashboard entry departs from the mockup-bound Settings body (recorded, task requirement wins).

### 2026-10-01 — Task 20 audit closure: a removed member can no longer merge a queued write — COMPLETE

- **The audit found one real server-side gap, and it was deeper than it first looked.** The Task 20 audit flagged that Phase 2 item 5 ("reject and never merge that member's queued mutations") was only partly enforced: `sync_can_write`'s author clause, `user_id = auth.uid()`, was checked before any firm helper, so a removed member could still push an **update** to a firm record they happened to author — and the phase note's claim that inserts/deletes were already refused was itself unverified. `20260930210000_sync_can_write_firm_membership.sql` replaces `sync_can_write` (the only write path a plpgsql body has) to close it.
- **The second defect is why the first went unnoticed — a SQL NULL trap.** The firm comparison was written `firm_id = current_firm_id()`. Once removal makes `current_firm_id()` NULL, that comparison is NULL, and `if not (<NULL>) then` does **not** branch in PL/pgSQL (`NOT NULL` is NULL, and a NULL condition is treated as "do not branch"). So the guard was permissive in exactly the case it existed for — a caller with no firm writing a row that has one — on **both** the INSERT and UPDATE paths. The fix replaces `=` with `is not distinct from` for every firm comparison, so a NULL on either side is a definite "no" rather than a slipped-through NULL; the `firm_id is null` disjunct still lets a personal row through.
- **Authorship no longer outlives membership, in all three places that trusted it.** A firm-scoped row may be written by its author only while that firm is still their firm (`firm_id is not distinct from current_firm_id()`); the RLS rule that an author may edit their own row (even without `can_edit`) is kept for current members. The same narrowing reaches a custom **reference** in a firm and a requester's own **pending delete request**, both of which were writable on `user_id` / `requested_by` alone. `can_edit_firm` / `can_delete_firm` still cover teammates and reviewers, and a `firm_id`-less personal row is untouched, so a removed member keeps their own diary. Only `sync_can_write` changed; `push_changes` already calls it.
- **Proven live, not just read.** `supabase/tests/push_changes_smoke_test.sql` gained a self-contained, rolled-back section: an associate (given their own premium entitlement so the refusal can never be the entitlement gate) authors a case and raises a request in the firm, proves the author rule still lets a **current** member edit their own row, is removed by the owner, and then has a queued **update**, a fresh **insert**, and a request **edit** all refused `permission_denied` with the rows provably unchanged — while the firm's owner can still edit the record. The first run of the smoke test exposed both defects (the NULL trap first, then the missing `is not distinct from`), which is exactly what a live check is for. The migration was applied to `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` (26 versions recorded) and refreshed directly with psql so the recorded version and the applied body agree; the ledger was regenerated (26 migrations, 575 KB) with its `0.0.330` group heading.
- **An offline guard so the live test is not the only witness.** `test/supabase/schema_contract_test.dart` gained a check that reads the new migration file directly (the `functionBlock` helper matches the first definition, which is the old file) and asserts every firm comparison uses `is not distinct from` and that none uses a plain `= public.current_firm_id()`. ### 2026-09-30 — Task 20 Phase 4 (server side): the approval is a queued update the server decides, against a target it locks — COMPLETE

- **The decision is server-side, and the client sends only an intention.** An approval is an ordinary queued update on `entity_type = 'delete_request'` whose payload sets `status = 'approved'`; `20260930200000_push_changes_delete_review.sql` replaces `push_changes` whole (the only write path a plpgsql body has) to teach that update what it means. Everything happens in the mutation's existing savepoint, so the tombstone, the request's resolution and the receipt either all land or none do. `rejected` is deliberately **not** special-cased: it keeps the record, sets the status and notifies the requester through the update the requester-side code already knows how to make.
- **Locking, in one order.** The request row is already locked `for update` by the generic update path; the branch locks the target next and only then decides. Request-then-target is the *only* order used, so two concurrent approvals for different requests can never deadlock, and no decision is made against a row that moves underneath it. Authorization is the reviewer's `can_delete_firm(request.firm_id)`, checked explicitly because `push_changes` is `security definer` and RLS does not run inside it — and a request whose target belongs to a *different* firm is refused, since a delete request is firm-scoped and a cross-firm target can only be tampering.
- **An old snapshot never authorizes deletion.** The request records the version its author saw (`target_base_version`). If the target now sits at a different version the approval is refused as `target_conflict`, and the request is parked as `status = 'stale_review_required'` **and** adopts the version the reviewer just saw — so a reconfirm needs no new client contract at all: resubmitting the same approval now compares against the row that exists. That is what makes `stale_review_required` a real state rather than a message. A target that is missing or already soft-deleted becomes `already_resolved` with its tombstone.
- **Interpretive choice, flagged.** On `already_resolved` the request is left **exactly as it was** (still `pending`, no reviewer, version unchanged) because no review actually happened — recording `approved`/`reviewed_by` for a decision that never took effect would put a false entry in the audit trail. The alternative (auto-cancelling it) would need a rule the task does not state. Say the word if you would rather it resolve itself.
- **Atomic success, and the target rides back.** Only an unchanged target is tombstoned: `is_deleted`/version/`last_modified_by`/`updated_at` on the target, the same `case_history` cascade an ordinary case delete performs, and the request's resolution (`status = 'approved'`, `reviewed_by`, optional `review_note`, server time) — one savepoint. The result carries `target` + `target_entity_type` (plus `children` for a case), so the reviewer's device applies the record's disappearance in the same pass instead of waiting for a pull. Duplicate submissions of the same mutation id return the stored receipt verbatim, so a retry can never tombstone twice.
- **The client change is small and deliberate.** `push_worker.dart` gained `_applyReviewTarget` (a no-op for every non-review result, since both fields are null) and routes the new `target_conflict` status through the same path as `already_resolved`: the updated request row and the current target row are applied and the queue entry resolves. It is **not** treated as a data conflict — nothing is frozen and no `conflict_log` row is written, because the server accepted the submission and recorded the staleness; a person resolves it by reconfirming, not by picking a winner. The task's rule that a completed review never resolves *another* queue entry is honoured: the target's own queued mutations are left untouched.
- **A real bug the live test caught, not the compiler.** My first cascade guard compared the request's stored `entity_type` (`'case'`) against `'cases'`, so the cascade silently did nothing on an approved case delete — the tombstone landed and the children stayed live. The smoke test's cascade assertion failed on the live database and the guard now tests the resolved *table*. Noted because it is exactly the kind of wrong-but-plausible comparison that reading the SQL would not have exposed.
- **Tests:** the `push_changes_smoke_test.sql` gained a delete-review section (self-contained, runs live inside its rolled-back transaction) covering a self-approval refused with the request and target untouched, an edit moving the target under the request → `target_conflict` + `stale_review_required` with the current row returned, the reconfirm tombstoning atomically and resolving the request with reviewer/note, a duplicate submission returning the identical receipt without a second tombstone, a case target cascading to its `case_history` child, an already-deleted target → `already_resolved` with no decision recorded, and a plain rejection keeping the record. Offline: 2 new in `test/sync/push_worker_test.dart` (an approval applies the target tombstone; a stale review applies both rows, freezes nothing and writes no `conflict_log` row) and 1 new schema-contract test asserting the branch's shape in the ledger. 1179 → **1182**.
- **Live, not just applied.** The migration was applied to `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` (25 versions recorded) and — after the cascade-guard fix — refreshed directly with psql so the recorded version and the applied body agree; the smoke test then ran green against the live database. - **One function decides, and nothing else does.** `delete_request_flow.dart`'s `deleteThroughFirmRules` is now the only place a case, a case-history entry, a note or a reference is deleted. It refreshes permissions first (the same `permissionFreshnessProvider` the other destructive confirmations call), then reads `canDeleteDirectlyProvider`: a member who may delete gets the ordinary window and the caller's own `deleteDirectly`; a member who may not gets a differently-worded window (*"Send A Deletion Request?"*, never *"Delete"*) and a queued `delete_requests` row plus the toast *"Deletion Request Sent To Admin/Owner."*. Wiring it here rather than in each screen is what stops the rule being applied on one screen and forgotten on the next; the four entity types are all covered (`case`, `case_history` in `case_detail_screen.dart`; `note` in `notes_screen.dart` and `note_detail_screen.dart`; `reference` in both the list's delete and the editor's save-then-delete path).
- **The request carries three real facts, none invented.** `createRequest` now takes a required `firmId` read from the cached profile — both the RLS insert policy and `sync_can_write` compare it to `current_firm_id()`, so a null there is a *refused* insert, not "no firm" — plus `entity_snapshot` (`deleteRequestSnapshot(row)`, the entity's own server-shaped row, which is what a reviewer reads and what proves the request meant *this* version) and `target_base_version` (`deletionBaseVersion(row.version)`, the version Phase 4 will compare against). It is queued through `sync_queue` under `entity_type = 'delete_request'` like any other push-domain row, which is what makes the workflow **offline-capable** (the task's item 2): nothing in the path touches the network.
- **The requester's own request can be re-snapshotted or withdrawn.** `refreshSnapshot` re-takes the snapshot and the observed version of a still-pending request (the record moved under it), and `cancel` withdraws it as a **soft** delete — `delete_requests` has no DELETE policy because the row is audit history. A request that was never pushed compacts away to nothing (insert + delete = a row the server never needed to know about); one the server has already seen becomes a tombstone. `watchMine(requestedBy)` scopes the list to its author for the UI Phase 4 will build.
- **A real defect found while making cancel-after-sync work, fixed for every push-domain table.** `SyncWriteHelper._record` read its prior mutations through `SyncQueueDao.getByEntity`, which returns **every** row the entity has ever had, `resolved` ones included — so a `resolved` insert counted as an open mutation. An entity whose first insert had already been pushed and resolved therefore swallowed every later change: a delete compacted to nothing at all (the server was never told), and an edit rewrote itself into a fresh *insert* the server would refuse as a duplicate id. The lookup now filters `state != 'resolved'`. This was not a delete-request bug — it applied to cases, notes and references too; it surfaced here because cancel-after-sync depends on the delete actually being queued. Pinned by two repository tests.
- **Honest scope note.** Phase 3's item 3 — "the requester can edit/cancel their own pending request" — is delivered at the **data layer** (`refreshSnapshot` / `cancel` / `watchMine`, RLS permits a requester's own pending update). There is deliberately **no requester-facing screen yet**: the approved plan places the requester list (`watchMine`) and the reviewer screen together in Phase 4, and the Settings main screen is mockup-bound (AGENTS.md rule 9), so a new entry point needs the user's sign-off on placement. Flagging rather than guessing.

### 2026-09-30 — Task 20 Phase 2: removing an associate revokes access in one statement, and the removed device erases itself — COMPLETE

- **The revocation is a relink, not a session kill.** `remove_firm_member(p_user_id uuid)` (`20260930190000_remove_firm_member.sql`, `SECURITY DEFINER`, owner-only, resolved from `firms.owner_id` rather than a parameter) deletes the `firm_members` row and sets the member's `profiles.firm_id = null`, `role = 'individual'`. That one update **is** the revocation, because every guard in this schema reads `firm_id`: `current_firm_id()` scopes every RLS policy, `can_edit_firm()`/`can_delete_firm()` gate `sync_can_write()` — so a removed member's queued mutations are refused and never merged — and `can_read_topic()` authorizes the `firm:{id}` Realtime topic. The auth session itself is left alone on purpose: this project has no service-role key, the task's item 5 says so, and the guard chain makes it unnecessary. Authored records are untouched — `user_id` and `firm_id` both stay — which is the Addendum's "preserve immutable audit attribution without reassignment", and nothing is ever reassigned to the owner.
- **The live run corrected one of my own assumptions, and the tests now say the true thing.** The first end-to-end check asserted that a removed member reads none of the firm's rows and **failed**: `cases_select_scoped` is `user_id = auth.uid() or firm_id = current_firm_id()`, so a removed member still sees the rows they authored — which is exactly what preserving attribution means — and loses the firm's *other* rows. The committed section now asserts both halves (their own row still visible, the owner's row not visible), plus `can_read_topic('firm:…')` false, `not_found` on a second removal, `cannot_remove_self`, a non-owner refused with the membership intact, and `anon` denied EXECUTE.
- **A DELETE fires no row trigger, so the announcement is explicit.** The RPC sends two Broadcast pings itself — `user:{removed}` (their own topic is always readable, including after the relink, so their devices learn at once) and `firm:{firm}` (every remaining member's roster) — both as the trigger's own `row_change` event, so the client needs no second decoder. The same migration attaches the *existing* `broadcast_row_change()` to `firm_members`, which covers the other half of the phase: a permission toggle now reaches the member it affects.
- **On the client a membership ping is routed, never pulled.** `firm_members` is a pull-only cache and not one of the twelve synced tables, so `syncEntityForTable` returns null for it and the ordinary path would drop it; `RealtimeListener` therefore gained `onMembershipChange`, fired **at most once per window** however many frames arrived, and `sync_providers.dart` points it at the account refresh. That refresh is also the removal detector, and the evidence is deliberately durable rather than in-memory: `profiles.firm_id == null` (the server's current answer) **while a cached `firm_members` row still exists** (what this device last knew) can only mean one thing, it survives a restart, and it is invisible to an individual, to a live firm member, and to a device whose caches have already been cleared. `MembershipRevokedScope` latches on that and replaces the app; one action runs Task 19's **own** `wipeAndComplete()` (the complete children-first wipe, `sync_queue` included — which is what "discard or roll back the pending local mutations" reduces to) and then signs out. **Nothing is erased until the user taps**: the erasure is the irreversible step, so it is announced first, and no safety copy is taken — the task asks for the queue to be discarded, and the authored records live on the server.
- **The notice that had no consumer finally has one.** `SyncService.notice` has carried `permissionsChanged` and `clockSkew` since Task 18 with nothing in `lib/` rendering either, so a provisional edit rolled back by a permission change was silent and a skewed clock mis-stamped everything quietly. `SyncNoticeBanner` reads them through a new `syncNoticeProvider` and is mounted in the same two places the conflict banner is; it is **dismissible** where the conflict banner is not, and that difference is the design — a conflict is frozen work that still needs a person, a notice explains something sync has already finished with. An empty notice renders nothing at all, so neither host has to ask.
- **Manage Associates grows the rest of the owner's toolset.** Outstanding unused invites are listed (named by their creation date — only the code's SHA-256 is stored, so the plaintext is genuinely unrecoverable) and can be revoked behind a confirmation, because the associate holding the code cannot be told what it was. Tapping a member opens a sheet with the role pair (`associate`/`viewer` — `owner` is not a choice, since ownership is `firms.owner_id` and not a row flag), the three permission flags, and a **Remove From Firm** action behind a confirmation that names the cost. The owner's own row opens nothing, deliberately: a flag on their `firm_members` row would not change what they may do. Every write invalidates the roster rather than caching it, so the screen stays a read of the firm's server state.
- **Permission freshness before a destructive action.** `permissionFreshnessProvider` runs the same single `accountRefreshProvider` entry point the launch/resume/reconnect hooks use, and is wired in front of the five destructive delete confirmations that exist today (case, case history, note from the list, note from detail, reference). It is a **no-op offline**, on purpose: blocking the action would take away the provisional offline workflow the plan requires, and `push_changes` is authoritative either way. It is also a no-op for an individual, whose own diary cannot change under them. Phase 3's single delete decision point will call this same helper.
- **A destructive provisional action is now visibly marked.** `isDestructiveQueueOperation()` names the one place that decides what counts as destructive, and Sync Status renders a red **Deletion Pending** pill beside the state pill for a queued delete. The state pill alone said `pending`, which is true of every queued rename too. *Flagged interpretive choice:* the marker is on the queue row rather than on the (already locally soft-deleted, therefore invisible) case or note — moving it onto the record itself would mean unfiltering every case-list query, which is a larger change than this phase should make unasked. ### 2026-09-30 — Task 19 Phase 5: a firm device that stayed away too long now rebuilds before it can write — COMPLETE

- **Firm mode only, per your instruction, and it is the right line.** The risk the lock exists for is *another writer* deleting a row while this device was away, so the device cannot tell a row it never saw from one the firm removed — and pushing would resurrect it (Sync Plan §3). An individual diary has one author, so nothing can have been deleted behind it, and locking a single-author device out of its own edits is pure harm. `shouldRecover` therefore requires firm mode, the whole flow — lock, safety copy, wipe — is skipped for an individual account, and **no server work happens for one either**. This is a deliberate narrowing of the plan's Phase 5 wording, which made no mode distinction in the task file and only a loose "premium/Firm mode" in §3. It is now recorded as a *Resolved Design Clarification* in `docs/implementation_plan.md` — **"Extended-Offline Recovery Lock Applies to Firm Mode Only (150 days, per-device)"** — with the plan's own §3 sentence and its summary bullet corrected in the same pass (so a later review cannot re-report the firm gate as a gap), a matching clarification note under the task file's Phase 5 heading, and the §3 `SharedPreferences` note corrected to the durable `sync_metadata` placement the Revision 2.4 Addendum requires.
- **The check is per-device and is never the profile's number.** `lib/sync/recovery_lock.dart` compares **this device's** own `last_successful_sync_at` against a 150-day threshold (the plan's 30-day buffer under the server's 180-day tombstone retention). `profiles.last_successful_sync_at` is deliberately not read: another device's recent sync would hide exactly the gap being looked for. A device that has never synced is not locked — a fresh install is what the initial pull is for. `lib/sync/recovery_flow.dart` runs the check when the cached profile arrives and when connectivity returns, and it catches its own failures so a check that cannot run never breaks a launch.
- **The lock is committed before anything else, and it survives being killed.** `RecoveryLock.engage` writes the flag **and** the checkpoint in one `sync_metadata` transaction, before any export or network work, and both are read back from the database rather than held in memory — so a device killed mid-recovery comes back locked. Proceed re-stamps the checkpoint inside the same transaction as the wipe. `SyncService._isEntitled()` refuses every run while the lock is set, which is what pauses both workers on the ordinary paths.
- **The blocking screen is the whole app.** `RecoveryRequiredScope` renders the app untouched when the lock is off and replaces it entirely when it is on, so there is no screen to edit, no FAB to press and no route to reach one — the plan's "editing/FAB disabled with a recovery-required message", done completely. It is an overlay rather than a route because it must sit above every screen including the one the app opens on, and must return on the next launch without navigation. Its passphrase fields are inline rather than the Backup screen's shared dialog, because this widget sits above the app's navigator and has none to show a dialog on; the labels are the shared ones.
- **Everything is exported before anything is erased, and the copy is verified before the wipe.** `BackupRepository.exportSnapshot` is the Task 15 path, so the safety copy is the same versioned encrypted container every other export writes — and its `backupTableOrder` already covers all 21 tables, `sync_queue` (the pending, blocked and conflicted rows) and `sync_metadata` included. The only difference is the destination: a new `LocalArchiveSink` writes into the app's own `documents/backups` directory instead of through a Save-to dialog, because the app is locked and nobody is there to answer one. **Proceed** re-reads the file, compares its checksum, and refuses to erase anything if it does not match — the passphrase is never generated or stored, since an archive nobody can open would be worse than none.
- **The wipe is one transaction, and only a completed rebuild clears the lock.** Every table is emptied children-first in a single durable transaction; the only thing preserved is the safety copy's own receipt (`archive.path`/`checksum`/`state`), because it describes a file outside the database and is what Proceed verifies against on a retry. Then the seed ledger is re-run, then a full authenticated pull from the sentinel, and only then is the flag cleared — so any failure anywhere leaves the lock set and the flow simply starts again. No session material is held in the database at all (the signed-in session lives in platform storage, which is never touched), so nothing has to be carried across and no reauthentication step is needed.
- **One honest limit, recorded rather than hidden.** The write guard lives in `SyncWriteHelper._record` — the single place every queued mutation passes through — which is *after* a repository's own Drift write. A repository reached through some non-UI path therefore leaves an unsynced local row behind when the guard throws. It is harmless in this flow (recovery erases every table, so nothing survives it), and it is marked with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and the upgrade path (hoist the guard to the repository entry points) rather than pretending the rejection is stricter than it is.

Both workers call it and neither keeps its own copy of the conflict logic (`push_worker._logConflict`/`_encode` are gone, `pull_worker`'s inline log write is gone). The verdict itself is pure and testable without a database: `lib/sync/conflict_rebase.dart`'s `planConflictRebase(base, server, local, changedFields)`. It compares against the mutation's **own** `changed_fields` when present and falls back to every differing field for an older row, ignores the bookkeeping columns every write touches (`id`, `version`, `updated_at`, `synced_at`, `server_updated_at`, `last_modified_by`, `created_at`, and `is_deleted`, which is answered by the tombstone verdict before any field comparison), and reports one of three verdicts.
- **Disjoint edits rebase themselves; nothing else does.** A disjoint change is laid over the authoritative row and re-sent as a **new** mutation — fresh `mutation_id` (the rejected one already has a server receipt, so replaying it would return the same rejection), `base_version` = the server's, the server row as both the new base and the rollback snapshot — and the entity never freezes. The conflict is still written to `conflict_log`, but already answered (`resolution_state = 'rebased'`, `resolved_at` set, `mergeable_conflict = true`), so it is an audit trail rather than a to-do. Overlap — the same field changed to two values — and **coupling** stay for a person: `syncFieldGroups` names the three field sets that are one logical value (the next hearing step's `next_date`/`last_step`/`notes_results`, the case identity, the filing details), so editing any one of a group is editing the group. Those, and **every tombstone**, freeze the entity (`conflict_pending`) and preserve every later queue entry.
- **The user's answers are three, and all three are explicit.** The Review Conflict screen (`lib/features/sync/presentation/review_conflict_screen.dart`) shows the server value and the attempted value for each colliding field, the editor's name resolved from the same-firm `profiles` cache via the server row's `last_modified_by` (never invented — the fallback is "Another Device"), and the later queue entries the freeze is preserving. `resolveWithFields` sends one new mutation against the server's version; `rebaseOntoNewRecord` copies the local work onto a **new** id (server-owned columns cleared, timestamps reset, queued as an insert) so a deleted row is never resurrected; `discard` rolls the authoritative row back into place behind a confirmation. Only `ConflictLogDao.setResolution` writes `resolution_state`, so a **dismissal or elapsed time can never look like a resolution** — pinned by test.
- **The banner is app-wide and non-dismissible.** `SyncConflictBanner` watches `ConflictLogDao.watchUnresolved()` and renders nothing at all when the list is empty. It sits **above the bottom navigation bar** inside `CasesScreenModal` (every case-list screen), and `AppShellRoot` renders it for the shell screens that have no nav bar — the two are mutually exclusive by route, so no screen shows it twice and none shows none. Tapping it pushes the Review screen, so Back returns where the user was.
- **`mergeable_conflict` from day one, local and mirrored.** Drift `schemaVersion` 9 → 10 with `if (from < 10) m.addColumn(...)`; `supabase/migrations/20260930160000_conflict_mergeable_column.sql` adds the column (`not null default false`, the safe direction) plus its comment; the mirror payload carries it on both the insert and every later resolution update, so a conflict raised on one device reads as answered on another instead of being recomputed there. The **90-day tombstone purge guard** the task also asks for was already implemented (`purged only when synced_at IS NOT NULL AND synced_at >= updated_at`); it now has a regression test instead of only a comment.
- **A real server defect, found by adding the mirror to the smoke test.** `push_changes` strips the client's `created_at` for `conflict_log` (the column is a server `timestamptz` defaulted to `now()`) and then put the client's epoch milliseconds straight back whenever the table had a `created_at` column at all — `jsonb_populate_record` cast `1790757617282` into a `timestamptz`, raising `22007`, which the per-mutation handler turns into a **permanent rejection**. So **no conflict mirror could ever land**: a conflict raised on one device was never reviewable on another. Caught by adding a `conflict_log` row to `supabase/tests/push_changes_smoke_test.sql` and running it, not by reading the function. `supabase/migrations/20260930170000_push_changes_created_at_guard.sql` replaces the function with one corrected condition — the fallback now also requires the column's **type** to be an epoch-ms integer — and both migrations are applied live on `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau`, recorded in `supabase_migrations`, with the ledger regenerated (22 migrations). The smoke test then passes end to end: the insert lands with `mergeable_conflict = true`, and a later update by `id` lands `user_resolved`.
- **Tests:** 40 new — 8 in `test/sync/conflict_rebase_test.dart` (both sides kept on disjoint fields; the same field twice differing needs a person; the same value twice does not; two fields of one step are coupled; a tombstone is never merged whatever the fields say; bookkeeping columns never make a conflict; an empty change list falls back to every differing field; an absent value and a null are the same value), 8 in `test/sync/conflict_resolution_test.dart` (the three reconcile verdicts, `resolveWithFields`, `rebaseOntoNewRecord`, `discard`, and that a dismissal never resolves), 5 in `test/database/tombstone_purge_test.dart` (purged only when synced and older than 90 days; an unsynced tombstone survives 400 days; a tombstone edited after its last sync survives; a recent one is kept; live rows are never touched), 5 in `test/features/sync_conflict_review_test.dart` (no conflict means no banner; one conflict shows the count and opens the screen with both candidate values; an answered conflict never reaches the banner; Save writes one replacement mutation, clears the banner and marks `user_resolved`; a tombstone offers only the two explicit answers and the copy lands as a new insert), plus the rewritten push/pull worker conflict tests (an overlap freezes; a **disjoint** conflict rebases itself and needs no person). **Protocol:** `flutter analyze` clean; full `flutter test` **1084 passed**; `test/supabase/` 75 passed; `push_changes_smoke_test.sql` `SMOKE OK` against the live project; ledger `--check` clean; `python tool/record_version.py --check` clean. ### 2026-09-30 — Task 19 Phase 2: a dropped socket is now retried on a ladder, and a resume pull is skipped only when continuity is proven — COMPLETE

- **The ladder, and where it stops.** `lib/sync/sync_health.dart` owns the reconnect schedule (1s → 2s → 4s → 8s → 16s → 32s, 63 s total, plan §1) and `SyncHealthController` drives it off the listener's status rather than off the socket, so an automatic re-join and a refused join are treated the same way. Past the last rung active retrying stops **on purpose**: retrying then would be polling, so the `connectivity_plus` stream, the next resume, or the user's tap is what restarts it. The ladder also stops while the app is backgrounded or the link is down (`setForeground`/`setOnline`), because retrying into a dead socket is exactly the waste §12.3 forbids.
- **The paused indicator is real, and tapping it does something.** After three consecutive failures — a push, a pull or a lost channel all count — the header's existing sync button shows the `SyncState.paused` state and its "Sync paused" tooltip (both already in the ARB). Tapping calls `SyncService.retryNow()`, which clears the service's own backoff window **and** the channel's ladder, rejoins, then runs a forced push-then-pull so a manual retry is never swallowed by the backoff the user is trying to escape. The button was dead before this phase (`SyncState.idle` and `isPremium: false` in every host); it now reports the live engine through `syncHealthProvider` and the single entitlement derivation, with the host's own parameter still honoured as an override.
- **The 60-second throttle now means something.** `canSkipResumePull()` requires **all three**: a full pull has succeeded before, the **same Realtime generation is still subscribed** (so no disconnect, re-join, channel error or fresh join happened in between), and that pull is inside 60 s. Elapsed time alone never skips a pull — Broadcast is ephemeral, so uncertain continuity is always repaired through REST. A skipped resume still asks for a push-only run, so anything queued while the app was away leaves immediately and costs no request when the queue is empty. One deliberate reading is worth recording: the channel is **not** closed on `inactive` (a call, the app switcher, a system dialog) — only on `paused`/`hidden`/`detached`, which is what "backgrounded or the screen locked" means in the plan. Closing on `inactive` would break continuity on every trip to the switcher and make the throttle dead code.
- **Gap repair is the drain's own order, now wired to the reconnect.** Connectivity restoration and every resume reset the ladder, rejoin, then push pending work and force a per-table delta pull; health is recorded as successful only after that pull commits, together with the generation it committed under — the pair the throttle reads next time.
- **Tests:** 11 new — 9 in `test/sync/sync_health_test.dart` (the default ladder is the plan's six rungs and 3-failure threshold; a failed join waits on each rung before retrying, proven with a 100 ms/600 ms schedule so a busy loop would fail it; active retrying stops after the last rung and stays quiet; three failures pause sync and a success clears them; a lost channel counts as a failure while a re-join only ends the ladder, never claiming a sync success; `retryNow` resets everything and joins immediately; leaving the foreground stops the ladder and returning attempts immediately; losing the link stops it and regaining it re-joins) and 2 in `test/sync/sync_service_test.dart` (a successful pull makes a resume skippable, and a re-join — a new generation — makes the next resume pull all twelve tables again). **Protocol:** `flutter analyze` clean; `flutter test test/sync/` **93 passed**; full suite **1057 passed**. Version `0.0.317`.

### 2026-09-30 — Task 19 Phase 1: a firm's edits now announce themselves, and a ping is only ever a hint — COMPLETE

- **The server half already existed, so this phase is client-only.** Task 16 Phase 3's `broadcast_row_change()` fires a `{table, id}` Broadcast ping from **all twelve** domain tables (including `court_categories`, which is the Addendum's requirement) to the row's private topic — `firm:{firm_id}` or `user:{user_id}` — and the `realtime_messages_read_own_topics` policy on `realtime.messages` is live on `lsthasywrdrhuuxnykau` (checked with `pg_policies`, not assumed). A failed ping pull is swallowed: the resume/reconnect delta pull is what repairs the gap.

Phase 2 is what consumes it.
